operator_plays.name: Public-Record & API Intelligence
operator_plays.mechanism: Ingest fragmented county dockets, probate registries, unclaimed property ledgers, and public APIs to surface uncontested claims or high-intent B2B triggers before manual competitors.
inputs: Court & probate dockets
State controller ledgers
Public licensing & entity APIs
workflow: Poll and normalize county/state record releases on an automated cadence
Cross-match entity/kinship/lien records and filter by minimum net fee threshold
Route verified dossiers into compliant outreach and claim execution
metrics: Cost per verified lead
Docket-to-contact latency (hours)
Net recovery / conversion rate

platform_risks.trigger: High-frequency automated polling against county or agency web portals
platform_risks.impact: Delayed lead ingestion or temporary IP block on target registry
platform_risks.detection_metric: HTTP 429/403 rate and daily record ingestion delta
platform_risks.fallback: Switch to scheduled bulk FOIA/public-record exports, official data feeds, and low-frequency cached queues

operator_plays.name: Distressed Asset Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Locate mispriced, orphaned, or administratively stranded assets—tax-sale overages, unclaimed state funds, dormant judgments, government surplus lots, or distressed micro-businesses—and capture a contingent recovery fee or acquisition spread.
inputs: Tax-sale excess proceeds ledgers
Unclaimed property & judgment dockets
Surplus auction manifests
workflow: Audit statutory fee caps, claim windows, and chain-of-title encumbrances
Execute skip-tracing or asset inspection to confirm net realizable value
Lock in contingent recovery agreements or below-intrinsic buyouts
metrics: Gross spread / contingent fee per case
Claim approval rate
Days from filing to disbursement

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory fee-cap compression or administrative hold
platform_risks.trigger: Jurisdiction updates finder fee limits, waiting periods, or filing documentation rules
platform_risks.impact: Reduced net fee margin or extended cash conversion cycle
platform_risks.detection_metric: County/state rejection notice rate and days-to-payout variance
platform_risks.fallback: Diversify across multi-state dockets and use attorney-backed filing partnerships where required

operator_plays.name: B2B Class-Action & Antitrust Settlement Contingency Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Monitor multibillion-dollar corporate antitrust and commercial class-action settlement funds (payment-card interchange, freight, auto parts, commercial insurance, SaaS) where 85–90% of eligible small businesses never file, and recover verified payouts on a 25–33% contingency fee.
inputs: Active federal B2B class-action settlement docket calendar & claims-administrator portals
B2B merchant-processing, fleet, & vendor spend intake pipeline
Contingency claim-preparation & court-authorized third-party filing agreements
workflow: Track open and upcoming commercial class-action settlements with verified court-appointed claims administrators and $50M–$5B+ settlement pools
Sign zero-upfront-cost (25–33% contingency) authorization agreements with operating restaurants, medical practices, retailers, and fleets
Extract historical merchant statements or vendor invoices, submit audited claim packages to the settlement administrator, and reconcile fee splits upon disbursement
metrics: Average gross settlement recovery per enrolled business ($5,000–$150,000+)
Claim acceptance rate by court-appointed administrator (%)
Net contingency fee per operator hour invested

platform_risks.failure_mode: Claim rejection, administrator audit hold, or court cap on third-party filer fees
platform_risks.trigger: Submitting unsubstantiated spend estimates, missing court bar dates, or failing to include required third-party filer disclosures
platform_risks.impact: Delayed payout disbursement or court-mandated fee reduction
platform_risks.detection_metric: Deficiency-notice rate (<2% target) and 100% court-approved disclosure compliance
platform_risks.fallback: File strictly for verified operating businesses with primary processor/vendor statements and use court-approved third-party claim-filing riders

operator_plays.name: State Treasury Escheatment & Unclaimed Corporate Warrant Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Ingest state controller/treasury escheatment ledgers and uncashed municipal/corporate warrant registries above $25,000, cross-match corporate officers via Secretary of State filings, and execute statutory recovery agreements for a 10–25% contingent finder fee.
inputs: State controller/treasury escheatment bulk ledgers
Uncashed municipal warrant & vendor-credit registries
Secretary of State officer & FEIN cross-match index
workflow: Filter state unclaimed-property and uncashed-warrant ledgers for high-value corporate and estate accounts exceeding $25,000
Resolve active corporate officers, successor entities, or authorized fiduciaries via SOS and skip-trace databases
Execute state-compliant finder agreements with statutory fee caps and submit notarized claim packages to the treasury administrator
metrics: Average gross warrant/escheatment claim size ($25k+)
Treasury claim approval rate (%)
Days from notarized filing to state disbursement

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory finder-fee cap violation or waiting-period rejection
platform_risks.trigger: Charging above state statutory fee limits (e.g., 10% in CA/FL/NY) or soliciting claims during restricted post-escheatment windows
platform_risks.impact: Voided recovery contract, state controller rejection, or administrative penalty
platform_risks.detection_metric: State-by-state fee-cap compliance check (100% pass) and claim rejection notice rate
platform_risks.fallback: Enforce per-state statutory fee caps and waiting-period rules in intake templates and disclose the owner's right to claim directly for free

operator_plays.name: Automated Parcel, LTL Freight & Tariff Overcharge Contingency Auditing
operator_plays.mechanism: Ingest mid-market shippers' UPS/FedEx/LTL EDI billing feeds and CBP Form 7501 customs entry summaries via read-only API to programmatically flag late-delivery SLA refunds, dimensional-weight billing errors, and duty-drawback refunds on a 35–50% contingency split.

CBP ACE Form 7501 customs entry & HTS tariff schedules
Automated carrier dispute & duty-drawback claim submission engine

Flag guaranteed-service late deliveries, duplicate accessorial fees, residential surcharges, and eligible export duty drawbacks
Auto-file carrier credit disputes and customs drawback claims, billing the client strictly 35–50% of verified credits posted to their statement
metrics: Recovered credits as % of total annual parcel/freight spend (2–8% target)
Dispute acceptance rate by carrier/customs (%)
Monthly recurring contingency revenue per shipper account

platform_risks.failure_mode: Carrier anti-automation lockouts or GSR (Guaranteed Service Refund) waiver clauses
platform_risks.trigger: Carriers inserting GSR waiver riders into custom shipper pricing agreements or throttling automated dispute bots
platform_risks.impact: Reduction in late-delivery refund volume on waived accounts
platform_risks.detection_metric: Claim approval ratio per carrier and % of audit recovery derived from billing/dim-weight errors vs. GSR
platform_risks.fallback: Pivot audit rules toward non-waivable dimensional-weight, duplicate-charge, LTL freight class, and contract-rate benchmarking recoveries

operator_plays.name: Out-of-Network Medical Claim & ERISA Appeal Contingency Recovery

Automated ERISA plan-document demand & Federal IDR portal filing workflow

Cross-reference payer remittances against statutory Open Negotiation windows (30 business days) under the No Surprises Act and ERISA SPD timelines
Generate evidence-backed arbitration briefs and ERISA appeals, collecting 20–35% of the incremental insurer payout above the initial remittance

IDR / ERISA appeal win rate vs. initial payer offer (%)
Contingency revenue per practice partner per month

platform_risks.failure_mode: Missed 30-day Open Negotiation / 4-day IDR initiation statutory deadlines or HIPAA breach
platform_risks.trigger: Failing to file within strict federal No Surprises Act business-day windows or handling PHI without a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA)
platform_risks.impact: Permanent forfeiture of IDR arbitration eligibility on expired claims or HIPAA compliance penalties
platform_risks.detection_metric: 100% BAA execution before EDI ingestion and automated T-minus-5-day statutory deadline alerts
platform_risks.fallback: Enforce HIPAA-compliant encrypted EDI pipelines with signed BAAs and fall back to longer-window ERISA administrative appeals when IDR windows have lapsed

operator_plays.name: Automated Commercial/Residential Property-Tax Appeal Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Ingest county tax-assessor valuation rolls upon annual notice release, run an automated valuation model (AVM) flagging parcels assessed above comparable neighbor equity ratios, and file bulk administrative tax protests for 30–50% of the first year's verified tax reduction.

Equity-ratio & recent-sale comparable AVM engine
Bulk administrative ARB (Appraisal Review Board) protest filing & hearing pipeline

Mail personalized pre-filled protest postcards showing the owner's exact estimated over-assessment and a QR code to sign a zero-upfront-cost contingency authorization
Auto-generate uniform comparable-equity evidence packets, file bulk administrative protests before the county bar date, and collect 30–50% of Year-1 tax savings

Percentage of appealed parcels receiving an assessment reduction (65–85% target)
Average net contingency fee per residential ($150–$450) and commercial ($2,000–$15,000) parcel

platform_risks.failure_mode: State property-tax consultant licensing requirements or missed county protest bar dates
platform_risks.trigger: Representing property owners for a fee without required state registration (e.g., Texas TDLR Property Tax Consultant license) or missing the 30/45-day county filing deadline
platform_risks.impact: Rejected bulk filings, administrative fines, or zero contingency revenue for the tax year

operator_plays.name: Transferable Federal & State Tax Credit Brokerage & Syndication (IRA § 6418 / Film / Historic)
operator_plays.mechanism: Scraping federal DOE/EPA interconnection queues, state film offices, and historic-preservation registries to originate transferable tax credits (IRC § 6418 Clean Energy Investment/Production Credits, Georgia/Louisiana Film Credits, State Historic Rehab & Brownfield Credits) from cash-strapped project developers at $0.82–$0.88 on the dollar and flipping them in simultaneous escrow closings to corporate and HNW taxpayers at $0.92–$0.96 on the dollar.
inputs: State film-office production certifications, National Park Service Part 2/3 Historic Preservation filings, and utility solar/biogas/storage interconnection queues
IRS Energy Credits Online pre-filing registration verification and tax-credit recapture insurance underwriting partners
Outbound network of CPA managing partners, corporate tax directors, and family-office CIOs with $1M–$50M+ in quarterly federal/state tax liabilities

Lock up exclusive purchase or placement options at $0.83–$0.89 per $1.00 of credit prior to quarterly corporate estimated tax deadlines (April 15, June 15, Sept 15, Dec 15)
Package the credits with a third-party CPA cost-segregation/eligibility opinion and tax-credit recapture insurance policy

Execute a simultaneous bilateral escrow closing with a corporate taxpayer at $0.92–$0.95 on the dollar—saving the buyer 5–8% guaranteed on their tax bill while capturing a 400–800 bps riskless spread ($40k–$80k per $1M block)

Net retained principal/brokerage spread (400–800 bps) per closed tranche
Days in escrow from developer IRS registration number issuance to wire settlement

platform_risks.failure_mode: IRS § 6418 recapture event or state department-of-revenue basis challenge
platform_risks.trigger: Project developer inflating eligible cost basis or taking a clean-energy asset out of service during the 5-year recapture window
platform_risks.impact: Taxpayer recapture assessment plus penalties if uninsured
platform_risks.detection_metric: 100% independent Big-4/national CPA cost-basis audit and mandatory A-rated tax-credit recapture insurance binder on every tranche
platform_risks.fallback: Never take unhedged balance-sheet inventory risk; close strictly via simultaneous back-to-back escrow funded by the buyer's wire and backed by non-cancelable tax-credit insurance

operator_plays.name: Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Schedule E/F Trade-Claim & Convenience-Class Rollups
operator_plays.mechanism: Purchase documented small trade claims below risk-adjusted expected plan distributions, accounting for objections, assignment procedures, and plan rules that may prohibit claim splitting or aggregation benefits.

3. Buy eligible claims through documented assignments and complete required transfer notices
4. Monitor objections and confirmation, then reconcile distributions to each acquired claim

Allowed claim value versus purchased face value
Realized return and days to distribution

platform_risks.impact: Reduced distribution or complete capital loss
platform_risks.detection_metric: Objection rate and eligible allowed value per portfolio
platform_risks.fallback: Stop affected purchases, enforce documented seller recourse where available, and price only supported general-unsecured recoveries

operator_plays.name: Out-of-Statute Charged-Off Debt Portfolio & Self-Serve Tradeline Settlement Funnels
operator_plays.mechanism: Evaluate heavily discounted time-barred receivables for lawful voluntary resolution, separating collection limitation periods from credit-reporting limits and excluding extinguished or otherwise uncollectible obligations.

Dispute records and credit-reporting eligibility dates

Net voluntary receipts after servicing costs
Dispute and disclosure-defect rate

operator_plays.name: State Film, Historic Rehabilitation (HTC) & Brownfield Transferable Tax Credit Placement

Transfer rules, recapture terms, and seller ownership records
Buyer state tax liabilities and escrow placement agreements

2. Have independent advisers validate eligible costs, ownership, liens, recapture exposure, and buyer utilization limits
3. Match approved buyers and sellers with disclosed pricing, fees, indemnities, and any available insurance exclusions
4. Complete required agency transfer approvals and escrow settlement, then retain filing and post-close monitoring records

Net placement fee per settled transaction
Transfer approval and escrow cycle days

platform_risks.failure_mode: Transfer rejected or purchased credit unusable

platform_risks.impact: Failed closing or buyer tax shortfall and indemnity dispute
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unresolved certificate exceptions and buyer utilization coverage

operator_plays.name: Automated Form 8850 WOTC (Work Opportunity Tax Credit) & Section 41 R&D Contingency Engine
operator_plays.mechanism: Automate employer-authorized WOTC screening and separately substantiate Section 41 research credits, earning outcome-linked service fees only where permitted; program authorization, qualifying activities, wage coordination, and professional fee restrictions govern each claim.

Research project evidence and qualified expense ledgers
State workforce certification procedures and tax-year credit and fee rules

2. Submit Form 8850 and required supporting forms within the applicable 28-day deadline and track state certification and qualifying hours
3. Separately document Section 41 qualifying research and expenses, reconciling wage overlap and applicable deduction adjustments with a tax professional
4. Obtain employer and preparer approval before filing, retain audit support, and collect permitted fees without guaranteeing credits

Substantiated credits realized by the employer
Net permitted service fees after review and filing costs

platform_risks.impact: Reduced credits, amended returns, penalties, and fee repayment exposure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Deadline exceptions, certification denials, and unsupported expense share
platform_risks.fallback: Exclude unsupported claims and use compliant fixed-fee payroll and research-documentation services under independent tax review

positioning_alternatives.title: The Corporate Lost-Asset Recovery Desk
positioning_alternatives.subtitle: Recover corporate uncashed warrants and dormant business balances with documented ownership chains and disciplined service-fee economics.
positioning_alternatives.audience: Bookkeeping firms, corporate records researchers, and recovery operators serving controllers with unresolved state-held business assets.
positioning_alternatives.research_basis: California Code of Civil Procedure sections 1540 and 1582 distinguish the owner's claim process from compensated recovery agreements. Build the service around entity continuity, authorized signers, supporting records, and jurisdiction-specific agreement requirements; never count the recovered corporate principal as operator revenue.

positioning_alternatives.title: The Evidence-First Property Recovery Practice
positioning_alternatives.subtitle: Win owner trust through verifiable treasury records, transparent finder agreements, and a clear direct-claim alternative.
positioning_alternatives.audience: Small research practices that can verify identity carefully and explain why an owner might purchase assistance instead of filing alone.
positioning_alternatives.research_basis: New York Abandoned Property Law section 1416 regulates agreements to locate abandoned property. California Code of Civil Procedure section 1582 supplies a separate agreement regime. Use state-specific fee and timing checks rather than exporting one state's contract nationwide, and disclose that owners can claim directly without purchasing recovery services.

positioning_alternatives.title: The Secure Claims Operations Pod
positioning_alternatives.subtitle: Combine record matching and claim-status tracking with tightly controlled identity evidence and exception handling.
positioning_alternatives.audience: Process-oriented founders building a three-person recovery pod before expanding to a five-person specialist operation.
positioning_alternatives.research_basis: California Civil Code section 1798.81.5 establishes reasonable-security requirements for covered businesses handling covered personal information. Pair its applicability assessment with the ownership evidence required by California's claim process. Automate candidate matching and reminders, while retaining human review of identity, signing authority, disputed ownership, and sensitive-document access.

chapters.question_prompt: What exactly is unclaimed property recovery, how is real operator revenue recognized vs underlying asset/client GMV, and what separates durable small-team moats from fragile beginner hype?
chapters.title: What Exactly Is Unclaimed Property Recovery?
chapters.subtitle: State-Treasury Claims, Corporate Uncashed Warrants, Finder-Fee Contracts, and Evidence-Led Recovery Under State Property Statutes
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #5, Unclaimed Property Recovery, holds Pipeline Rank #04 of 29 with an 89/100 Money-to-Manpower Score: an Elite Small-Team Cash Machine when evidence quality outruns acquisition expense. The business earns recognized service fees, never the owner's recovered asset value. This chapter maps 12 plays, separating treasury recovery from adjacent transferable-credit placement and showing where each requires different authority, contracts, and settlement controls. Canonical annual owner profit is $15,000 Conservative, $95,625 Base, and $225,000 Scaled. Durability comes from corporate identity resolution, successor documentation, lawful finder agreements, and disciplined claim tracking. Beginner hype comes from counting searchable balances as revenue, treating public names as verified owners, and charging for claims before statutory restrictions and collection conditions are satisfied.

key_metrics.note: 25% margin; $15,000 annual owner net profit; 1 FT + 2 C

key_metrics.note: 37.5% margin; $95,625 annual owner net profit; 1 FT + 2 C

sections.heading: 1. Sell Documented Recovery Work, Not Access to Public Money
paragraphs: Unclaimed property recovery is an evidence and administration business. A holder, such as an insurer, employer, bank, or vendor, retains an owner's property until the applicable dormancy and reporting rules require transfer to a state administrator. The recovery operator identifies a plausible owner, establishes authority, assembles the administrator's required documents, and follows the claim through payment. The state generally holds custodial property for its owner; a public listing does not transfer ownership to the person who finds it. Corporate uncashed warrants need another distinction: a stale government check may require reissuance by the issuing agency rather than a treasury claim, and some public obligations have separate deadlines. Determine the payer and legal route before quoting a fee. The owner's ability to claim directly without a recovery service belongs in the first substantive communication, not a buried attachment. Paid value comes from resolving an old address, locating merger documents, reconciling duplicate records, and reducing employee time. MissingMoney and official state portals are discovery interfaces, not exclusive inventory. A browser result establishes a lead; accepted ownership evidence establishes a claim; an enforceable earned fee establishes operator revenue.

Five operator archetypes organize this market: corporate treasury sweep specialists, successor-entity researchers, estate documentation coordinators, institutional entitlement tracers, and jurisdiction-focused claim administrators. Their economics differ because difficult authority chains can justify substantial service effort while straightforward consumer claims often cannot. A corporate sweep might identify twenty vendor checks under four historical company names; the moat is the verified relationship between those names and the current claimant. An estate specialist instead needs current representative authority and the correct succession route, not merely a death record. An institutional tracer must distinguish an insurance benefit, securities proceeds, and a deposit balance because each creates different evidence demands. Begin with $5,000–$35,000 startup capital and a 3–12 month first-deal planning horizon, rather than funding operations from expected approvals. The stated $1,500–$8,000 monthly operating expense range is a planning envelope for recurring operations, not proof that every staffing configuration fits inside it. Registration, permitted representation, fee ceilings, waiting periods, and privacy duties vary by jurisdiction. California Code of Civil Procedure section 1582 and New York Abandoned Property Law section 1416 illustrate why one national finder contract is a weak foundation.

This chapter's twelve mapped plays comprise two named cross-platform plays and ten concrete recovery applications. The named plays are public_record_api_intelligence and state_film_historic_brownfield_tax_credit_brokerage. The ten recovery applications are corporate treasury sweeps, vendor-check recovery, payroll-check recovery, refund recovery, insurance-proceeds recovery, securities-entitlement tracing, merger-successor recovery, probate representation support, dissolved-entity authority reconstruction, and multistate claim-status operations. These applications are operating lanes, not ten additional promises of separate income. Corporate sweeps organize the account; vendor, payroll, refund, insurance, and securities lanes classify the asset; successor, probate, and dissolution lanes resolve authority; status operations coordinate submission and collection. Public-record intelligence supplies evidence across those lanes. Transferable-credit placement is an adjacent brokerage discipline, not a treasury recovery claim, and must retain separate contracts, accounting, and eligibility checks. Do not add twelve projected income streams together when the same claim traverses several lanes. Assign one property identifier, one owner relationship, one collection event, and one service-fee ledger entry. The durable operator sells accountable completion of a difficult administrative task. The fragile beginner sells an impressive spreadsheet of balances that may belong to someone else.

callout.title: Win the Authority Chain Before Selling the Balance
callout.body: The strongest practitioners improve evidence yield and client trust before buying additional lead volume.
items: Ask corporate treasury for an approved historical-name and address schedule; reconcile every proposed match against that schedule before requesting sensitive documents.
Keep the original holder name and state property identifier together; similar dollar amounts do not prove that two portal records represent the same obligation.
Show the official direct-claim route in outreach, then price the research and coordination burden that the owner actually wants removed.
Separate stale municipal warrant reissuance from state-custody recovery; the issuing agency's procedure can control the result even when a treasury search is empty.

sections.heading: 2. Reconcile Service Fees, Collection Timing, and Owner Profit
paragraphs: The revenue boundary is recognized service fees, not client asset value. If an owner receives $50,000 and an enforceable agreement entitles the operator to a permitted 10% fee after successful recovery, the operator's revenue is $5,000, not $50,000. The remaining $45,000 is not an operator expense because the operator never earned that principal. Prefer payment directly from the administrator to the owner, followed by a separately supported service invoice. That route reduces custody exposure and clarifies the ledger without eliminating collection risk. Record discovered value, submitted value, approved value, owner-paid value, earned fees, invoiced fees, and collected fees as distinct measures. Under an accrual policy aligned with ASC 606, a contingent success fee requires analysis of the performance obligation and variable-consideration constraint; a search hit is never enough. A conservative operating policy recognizes the fee only after documented owner payment when that resolves the contractual contingency. Cash-basis reporting instead follows actual receipt under the applicable accounting method. Retainers and separate research charges need their own lawful terms and performance analysis; renaming a restricted finder fee does not remove the restriction.

The canonical cases reconcile without treating recovered principal as sales. Conservative revenue is $60,000, expenses are $45,000, and annual owner net profit is $15,000 at a 25% margin with 1 FT + 2 C. Base revenue is $255,000, expenses are $159,375, and owner net profit is $95,625 at 37.5%, again with 1 FT + 2 C. Scaled revenue is $450,000, expenses are $225,000, and owner net profit is $225,000 at 50% with 2 FT + 3 C, or five people. These are annual scorecard cases, not commitments about monthly cash availability. At an illustrative lawful 10% realized fee, the corresponding recovered client assets are $600,000, $2,550,000, and $4,500,000. That percentage is a modeling assumption, not a nationwide fee rule. The same revenue totals could arise from sixty $1,000 fees, eighty-five $3,000 fees, and ninety $5,000 fees respectively. Those averages imply different claim selection and evidence burdens, not automatic productivity improvements. Reconcile the annual expense envelope to researcher payments, payroll, verification, acquisition, insurance, software, and collection losses. Contractor headcount does not specify contractor hours, and owner profit is not an additional revenue category.

Use contribution arithmetic before hiring a researcher for a promising list. Suppose a qualified corporate claim yields a $3,000 collected fee, requires six hours at $45 per hour, and consumes $130 of document and account-servicing expense. Its $2,600 contribution precedes acquisition cost, shared overhead, and owner compensation treatment. If four equally expensive qualified files produce only one payment, the cohort spends $1,600 to collect $3,000, leaving $1,400 before those shared costs. Averages that exclude rejected files conceal the central risk. Conversely, a $200 owner balance at a 10% fee produces only $20; even twenty minutes of paid review can exhaust the economics. Direct such owners to the official portal unless a lawful batch engagement makes servicing efficient. Maintain a rolling thirteen-week cash forecast because document requests, probate issues, and administrator queues can defer collection for months. The startup range must support that delay without depending on owner funds. Reconcile the stated monthly operating envelope separately from the scorecard's total annual costs, especially at scale. Reserve for fee disputes and billing reversals where entitlement fails; do not inflate a supposedly high-margin model by ignoring unsuccessful work.

sections.heading: 3. Build a Sub-Vertical Evidence Moat Without Mixing Asset Classes
paragraphs: The public_record_api_intelligence play turns fragmented public records into a prioritized evidence queue, not permission to harvest every available personal detail. Combine official treasury ledgers, permitted county docket access, probate registries, secretary-of-state records, and documented public APIs where available. Many portals offer no public API; do not infer one from an internal browser endpoint. Store source URL, retrieval date, property identifier, historical address, and match rationale in SQLite or PostgreSQL. OpenRefine can standardize entity names, while explicit rules preserve differences between a parent, subsidiary, and unrelated business with a similar name. An illustrative authorized batch of 2,000 records might yield forty plausible matches and eight document-qualified claims averaging $12,500. At a lawful 10% realized fee, those eight successful payments would generate $10,000, not the $100,000 client principal. Before payment, that amount remains a contingent pipeline estimate. At $900 extraction cost and $1,800 review cost, the cohort leaves $7,300 before claim servicing and other expenses only if all eight pay. When access changes, switch to scheduled bulk FOIA or state public-record exports, official data feeds, and low-frequency cached queues rather than bypassing access controls.

The comparison matrix pairs actual discovery interfaces with claim types rather than implying that every portal exposes every useful field. California's Controller, New York's Comptroller, ClaimItTexas, Florida Treasure Hunt, and other state systems differ in displayed amounts, identity checks, document delivery, and representative procedures. Capture the official property's type before asking for supporting records. A payroll claim may turn on an old residential address; a corporate vendor check may require proof that a former trade name belonged to the claimant; an estate claim may depend on court-issued authority. Historical addresses are corroboration, not substitutes for identity. Corporate acquisitions create especially useful research opportunities because public records preserve old names while employees lose institutional memory. They also create hard failures: a stock sale, statutory merger, and asset purchase do not transfer rights identically. Review transaction documents before asserting successor entitlement. For securities, establish whether the state holds shares or liquidation proceeds and explain the payable basis before computing fees. The moat is a reusable evidence map with bounded access and documented corrections, not a secret claim database that an owner could search free.

The state_film_historic_brownfield_tax_credit_brokerage play belongs beside recovery only as an explicitly separate placement service. It matches certified transferable state credits with eligible taxpayers at negotiated discounts; it does not locate an owner's escheated cash. For example, $100,000 of verified transferable state credit sold for $92,000 creates $92,000 of seller proceeds. A disclosed placement fee equal to 2% of those proceeds produces $1,840 of operator revenue when earned under the engagement, not $100,000. Buyer eligibility, vintage, use limits, transfer registration, and recapture exposure require program-specific review. Georgia's film-credit statute, O.C.G.A. section 48-7-40.26, provides one state-specific starting point; historic rehabilitation and brownfield programs require their own enabling provisions. Federal rehabilitation credits under 26 U.S.C. section 47 are not thereby freely saleable, and section 50 contains important recapture rules. The fallback is to suspend settlement under diligence contingencies and rematch only verified eligible credits without guaranteeing tax savings. Keep this hypothetical fee outside all three canonical recovery cases. Combining credit face value, discounted seller proceeds, recovered owner assets, and service fees would erase the very business-model distinction this chapter establishes.

sections.heading: 4. Operate an Evidence Queue That Survives Rejection and Distrust
paragraphs: Build the workflow around a case register and a restricted document store. Airtable can track non-sensitive case metadata; a properly configured Microsoft SharePoint or Google Workspace repository can hold supporting files with named access, multifactor authentication, and access logging. Product selection alone does not establish security. Separate lead researchers from identity-document reviewers, prohibit identity documents in ordinary spreadsheet attachments, and set retention periods against actual contractual and statutory requirements. Record the state's submission channel rather than uploading documents to whichever link appears in an email. Outreach should identify the operator, describe the service, disclose direct claiming, and explain how the recipient can verify the official record independently. Never impersonate a treasury office or imply that paying the operator is required to obtain property. Customer distrust is rational in this market; reduce it with verifiable identifiers, restrained contact frequency, and a clear written fee basis. Initial contact does not need a full identity packet. Request only the documents required for the next validated claim step, and direct submission to the state when its process permits that safer arrangement.

Automate record matching and claim status tracking, the two scorecard levers, while keeping judgment with accountable reviewers. Normalize punctuation and corporate suffixes for candidate generation, but never merge entities solely because normalization produces the same string. Require corroborating address, transaction, or legal-entity evidence before changing a match to qualified. Store the reviewer and rationale so a later rejection improves the rules instead of disappearing into a spreadsheet. Track explicit states: research, authority pending, agreement eligible, submitted, evidence requested, approved, owner paid, fee earned, and fee collected. Keep administrator status separate from internal billing status; approval may still precede payment or further validation. Use permitted notifications and scheduled human checks when no authorized machine interface exists. Do not evade portal rate limits to make an automation dashboard look current. Measure qualified-match yield, document rework, days between requested and received evidence, collection lag, and contribution per completed cohort. Identity mismatch, low claim values, and distrust should each have a measurable stop condition. Scale only after repeat cohorts demonstrate that fewer manual touches do not increase wrongful matches or uncollectible fees.

A practical first ninety days establishes a repeatable jurisdiction-and-account combination rather than a national claim factory. Select one state, one corporate property category, and a narrow owner profile with accessible authority records. Build the legal requirements sheet from primary statutes and current administrator instructions; record effective dates and revisit it before contracting. Test a small authorized record batch, manually review every proposed identity match, and ask prospective clients whether internal treasury staff already pursue these balances. Price against expected collected fees, including failed files, instead of advertised property totals. Move into a second jurisdiction only after the first process reliably produces complete submissions and auditable accounting. The pre-flight checks below are operating stop conditions, not ceremonial signatures. A missing authority document means no submission; an invalid fee arrangement means no contingent billing; a disputed ownership chain means no claim of certainty. The business earns its small-team advantage by declining weak files early and completing strong files cleanly. Its real asset is an evidence system that owners and administrators can trust, not the volume of money visible in public searches.

sections.heading: 1. Identify the owner, the economic buyer, and the person authorized to pay
paragraphs: The treasury is normally the asset custodian, not the buyer of your service. A named owner, authorized estate representative, or corporate successor hires the recovery firm and owes its permitted fee. Separate three roles before quoting: entitlement to the property, authority to sign the service agreement, and authority to release payment. A corporate controller may sponsor a claim while treasury controls incoming funds and accounts payable controls your invoice. An estate beneficiary may want speed but lack authority to bind the estate. Request the actual delegation, letters of appointment, or corporate signing policy rather than accepting an impressive title. No statute generally forces an owner to hire a finder. The acute pain is an unreconciled receivable, an estate that cannot close cleanly, missing merger evidence, or staff time diverted from higher-value work. State explicitly that the owner can claim directly through the state's official process without hiring your firm. Then sell a defined evidence package, submission support, and status tracking. A $40,000 corporate claim at an otherwise permitted 10% fee produces $4,000 of service revenue, not $40,000. The remaining $36,000 belongs economically to the owner after that fee.

Decision-maker psychology changes the sales process more than the size of the public listing. Individuals first ask whether the letter is a scam; corporate staff ask whether the asset really belongs to their entity; fiduciaries ask whether the expenditure can be supported in their accounting. Lead with an independently verifiable property record, the official agency contact, and a plain explanation of your separate business. Never request banking credentials to prove ownership. For a corporate uncashed warrant, determine whether the issuing agency can still reissue the warrant or whether custody has transferred to the state. The correct route changes the evidence, payee, and payment clock. Ask the controller to identify the general-ledger account, vendor-onboarding requirements, purchase-order threshold, and invoice approver before work starts. Ask an estate representative how recovery expenses are approved and whether distributions are already scheduled. Do not manufacture urgency from a nonexistent expiration date. Real urgency comes from a documented estate hearing, dissolution timetable, expiring supporting records, or a customer's reporting deadline. Put that date beside the agency's actual processing estimate, not beside a salesperson's promised settlement date. A trustworthy explanation of delay often converts better than a larger headline recovery estimate.

Screen willingness and ability to pay separately from entitlement. A valid owner can still be insolvent, disorganized, or determined to avoid the fee. Check entity status through the relevant Secretary of State, review authorized bankruptcy records through PACER when indicated, and obtain the customer's vendor-payment instructions directly. Public records are leads, not a complete credit opinion. Bankruptcy can change who controls an asset; pause owner-directed collection until counsel resolves estate ownership and representative authority. For ordinary corporate customers, confirm whether accounts payable will accept a contingent invoice supported by the treasury remittance advice. A purchase order documents internal purchasing authority but does not redirect treasury funds or override a finder statute. For individuals, agree on the invoice trigger and a lawful payment method without conditioning assistance on surrender of the entire recovery. Estimate collection exposure before buying records: a $1,000 expected fee with $250 acquisition cost, $200 document labor, and a 20% noncollection assumption leaves only $350 before general overhead. If the economics fail, decline the engagement or offer a lawful, clearly scoped alternative. Do not solve weak underwriting by taking control of a claimant's identity or account.

sections.heading: 2. Select a payment rail that preserves owner control and supports collection
paragraphs: Design two distinct money movements: custodian to lawful owner, then customer to recovery firm. The default should be direct state payment to the owner, followed by an invoice tied to the engagement's permitted earning event. Some jurisdictions provide a specific process for paying an authorized representative or allocating a permitted fee; use it only when the agency's rules and accepted documents support that exact route. Never assume a power of attorney creates an assignment, grants unlimited endorsement authority, or obligates a treasury to split a check. Record the claim identifier, approved amount, actual receipt date, invoice identifier, and fee calculation as separate fields. A claim marked approved is not collected cash, and a check mailed to an old address is not evidence that the owner received usable funds. Define the contractual payment trigger around verifiable receipt or another lawful, clearly specified event. If the agency pays by paper check, document deposit and settlement through an appropriate customer confirmation, not unrestricted account access. Preserve a narrow remittance extract rather than the owner's entire bank statement. That separation keeps client principal out of the firm's operating account and makes disputed calculations easier to resolve.

Choose the customer-to-firm rail by ticket size, payer type, reversibility, and administrative friction. ACH usually suits a business invoice, but a debit requires valid authorization and applicable network and account rules; an ACH credit initiated by the customer avoids storing debit instructions. Consumer preauthorized electronic transfers introduce specific requirements under 12 CFR 1005.10, including authorization and stop-payment rights where applicable. A card checkout through Stripe can simplify small invoices but adds processing charges and dispute exposure. Verify processor acceptance of the actual business model before using it. Fedwire is useful for larger business payments, although bank cutoffs, account verification, sanctions screening, and fraud procedures still matter. Do not describe any rail as eliminating all recovery or litigation risk. An independent escrow arrangement can coordinate an authorized settlement, but ordinary treasury claims rarely require an operator-controlled escrow account. Have the custodian confirm whether the proposed destination is permitted before promising escrow-based fee protection. For changed wire instructions, call a previously verified number and require independent internal review. Email alone is insufficient evidence of a new beneficiary account, even when the sender appears to be the established controller.

Retainers, factoring, and milestone holds are commercial structures rather than interchangeable bank networks. A retainer collected by ACH is still subject to the rules governing the underlying recovery agreement, including any restriction on advance compensation. Calling a recovery charge a research deposit does not remove a statutory fee ceiling. Milestones may support permitted fixed-scope document work, but they cannot turn a prohibited early fee into a lawful one. Factoring transfers or finances an eligible operator receivable; it does not create ownership of the customer's treasury claim. A factor will examine invoice validity, assignment terms, debtor credit, disputes, and recourse. On a $4,000 earned invoice, an illustrative 3% financing charge costs $120 before other contractual charges; that expense reduces contribution rather than increasing recovery revenue. Escrow has its own administrative costs and release conditions, so reserve it for permitted cases where the coordination benefit exceeds those costs. Establish a fallback before submission: if the agency rejects split disbursement, the owner receives the full award and pays through the agreed invoice rail. Do not reroute proceeds through an employee, nominee, unrelated affiliate, or newly opened account merely to preserve your expected fee.

sections.heading: 3. Protect the fee through enforceable scope, verified identity, and disciplined collections
paragraphs: Fee protection begins with a jurisdiction worksheet, not an aggressive noncircumvention paragraph. Identify the custody program, applicable finder registration, permitted contracting date, compensation ceiling, required disclosures, and any assignment restrictions before presenting terms. California Code of Civil Procedure section 1582 regulates recovery agreements, including timing and compensation; its 10% ceiling cannot be bypassed by splitting an invoice into discovery and administration charges. Texas Property Code section 74.507 supplies its own agreement requirements and compensation limitation. Apply the actual provision to the relevant property and transaction rather than copying a national contract template. Keep the official statutory text and agency instructions with a dated review record. If the applicable waiting period has not elapsed, do not secure a prohibited agreement now and simply postpone the invoice. Where registration is required, confirm that the firm and the individual performing regulated activity satisfy the relevant rules. The contract should identify the property or covered portfolio precisely enough to distinguish your assignment from unrelated assets. Define the fee base, treatment of partial payments, expenses, termination, and evidence of receipt. Avoid claiming perpetual rights over every future recovery an owner may discover independently.

Circumvention usually starts as an evidence problem: the customer believes the firm only copied a free listing, while the firm believes it built a complete entitlement package. Record the contracted deliverables and their delivery dates. Use DocuSign or Adobe Acrobat Sign to preserve signed terms and delivery records, but remember that an electronic signature does not cure an unlawful agreement. Give the customer a claim-specific progress log and copies of documents they are entitled to receive. A narrowly drafted fee obligation may remain payable when the owner receives the covered property directly, if local law and the agreement support that result. It should not penalize the owner's statutory right to claim without a finder. Distinguish a genuine refusal to pay an earned invoice from a dispute about identity, scope, calculation, or prohibited charges. Send a calculation with the initial invoice, a concise reminder after the agreed due date, and a written resolution proposal before escalating. Have counsel assess collection options and applicable consumer rules where relevant. Do not threaten criminal action, impersonate the treasury, or assert a lien that the firm does not possess. Clear documentation protects margin better than pressure tactics that create another dispute.

Identity quality determines whether the payment rail can work at all. A name match is an intake signal, not proof of ownership. Match historical addresses, entity identifiers, predecessor relationships, and claim-specific documentation against the agency's requirements. Resolve same-name conflicts before sending sensitive documents or quoting a recovery as certain. Collect only what the filing requires, use restricted-access storage, and keep identity evidence out of ordinary CRM notes. Airtable can track case status, while a separately controlled document repository holds sensitive attachments; assess the actual configuration rather than assuming a product name supplies security. Define retention periods around agency requirements, contractual evidence, and applicable privacy duties. Limit contractors to the cases and documents needed for assigned work. A counterparty credit review should also identify suspicious payment changes, third-party payment requests, and attempts to redirect an estate payment into a beneficiary's personal account without authority. Escalate ownership conflicts and suspected fraud instead of improving the paperwork around a questionable story. When the verified recovery is too small to cover document costs, provide the official direct-claim route and close the opportunity. Rejecting a low-value or mismatched claim preserves both customer trust and the team's available filing capacity.

sections.heading: 4. Reconcile the mapped plays to fee revenue, owner profit, and working capital
paragraphs: Treat distressed_asset_recovery as the operating family, not permission to apply one state's finder contract to every stranded asset. State unclaimed funds, tax-sale overages, dormant judgments, government surplus lots, and distressed micro-businesses have different ownership, filing, licensing, and valuation requirements. For this volume, the clean starting lane is documented treasury property and corporate uncashed warrants. Illustratively, $2,550,000 of eligible client recoveries at a permitted 10% fee produces the Base case's $255,000 annual service revenue. This is an equivalent-volume illustration, not a universal legal rate or forecast of approval. At an 8% realized rate, the same fee target requires $3,187,500 of eligible recoveries. A rejected claim produces no contingent fee, while a partial recovery shrinks the invoice base. Diversify across researched multi-state programs and dockets rather than concentrating every submission in one agency queue. Use attorney-backed filing partnerships where required, with properly structured compensation instead of informal sharing of professional fees. If an adjacent asset requires acquisition capital, litigation, or licensed representation beyond the firm's capability, refer or decline it. Do not present an acquisition spread as recovery service revenue inside this volume's canonical scorecard.

The adjacent play wotc_hourly_payroll_tax_credit_contingency_engine serves an employer, not a treasury-property claimant. Its WOTC component requires employer-authorized screening and timely certification procedures under 26 U.S.C. 51, including the generally applicable 28-day submission rule for Form 8850. Verify authorization for the worker's hire date; the statutory termination provision must be checked for any post-2025 extension rather than assumed away. Illustratively, ten eligible hires producing $2,400 each generate $24,000 of employer credits, not operator revenue. A hypothetical 15% outcome-linked charge would equal $3,600 only where the service and fee arrangement are permitted. Section 41 research credits require a separate factual analysis of qualified activities and expenditures, plus coordination of overlapping wage benefits; payroll volume alone proves neither eligibility nor credit size. A substantiated $40,000 research credit and a permissible 10% service fee would produce $4,000 of operator revenue. Evaluate applicable professional restrictions, including 31 CFR 10.27 where relevant, before offering contingent pricing. Exclude unsupported claims and fall back to compliant fixed-fee payroll or research-documentation services under independent tax review. Keep these adjacent examples outside the unclaimed-property revenue bridge unless a separately approved operating model explicitly includes them.

The canonical scenarios are service-fee economics: Conservative revenue of $60,000 less $45,000 of implied annual costs yields $15,000 owner profit at 25%; Base revenue of $255,000 less $159,375 yields $95,625 at 37.5%; Scaled revenue of $450,000 less $225,000 yields $225,000 at 50%. Staffing remains 1 FT plus 2 contractors in Conservative and Base, then 2 FT plus 3 contractors at Scaled. Do not assume contractor counts describe full-time utilization. At a $3,000 average recognized fee, the revenue targets require 20, 85, and 150 equivalent completed fee events annually. Recognition still follows the firm's applicable accounting policy; approval status alone does not establish earned revenue or collection. Maintain separate dashboards for expected recoveries, earned fees, receivables, and cleared cash. The stated $1,500 to $8,000 monthly operating range is not a substitute for the scenarios' complete annual cost budgets. Startup capital of $5,000 to $35,000 must bridge a possible three-to-twelve-month first-deal interval. Automate record matching and status tracking, then measure exception labor and days from owner receipt to fee collection. If cash lags, reduce acquisition spending before borrowing against speculative claims. Scale verified cases, not the nominal dollars displayed in public property listings.

chapters.question_prompt: What are the real unit economics, gross-to-net margin deductions, scrub/reversal reserves, and working-capital float requirements for unclaimed property recovery?
chapters.title: Unit Economics, Margin Waterfall & Working-Capital Float
chapters.subtitle: Treasury Finder-Fee Cohorts, Identity Scrubs, Contractor CAC, Settlement Holds, and Cash Conversion Under State Recovery Statutes
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #5, Unclaimed Property Recovery, holds Rank #04 with an 89/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. This chapter translates 12 mapped plays into a fee-only operating model: client property is never operator revenue. Conservative, Base, and Scaled cases produce $60,000, $255,000, and $450,000 recognized annual fees, yielding $15,000, $95,625, and $225,000 annual owner profit. The waterfall separates identity scrubs, fee reversals, contractor delivery, acquisition, overhead, and collection expense. Cash planning then adds treasury processing, payout restrictions, and invoice DSO rather than treating an accepted claim as spendable cash. Settlement recovery receives its own eligibility and fee logic; corporate class-action contingencies cannot be substituted for capped state finder fees.

sections.heading: 1. Define the Fee Unit Before Buying Another Lead
paragraphs: Start with a claim cohort, not the treasury search result count. A cohort contains files admitted during one acquisition period, each linked to an owner, property identifier, jurisdiction, permitted contract, and documented fee basis. For this illustrative bridge, Conservative processes 100 admitted files with $750 average potential fees; Base processes 300 at $1,000; Scaled processes 500 at $1,000. Their initial fee pools are therefore $75,000, $300,000, and $500,000. These are prospective contractual economics, not booked receivables. If a permitted 10% fee applied throughout, the corresponding potential client recoveries would be $750,000, $3,000,000, and $5,000,000. Those assets remain client property and never enter the operator revenue column. Ten percent is a modeling assumption, not a nationwide entitlement. California Code of Civil Procedure section 1582 constrains covered recovery agreements, while other states impose different conditions. Store the applicable rule version alongside each agreement. Exclude ineligible contracts before counting a file as monetizable. Separate the owner from the payee and the signatory: a corporate officer, estate representative, and individual claimant require different authority evidence even when names appear similar in the public property record.

Define the economic denominator consistently. The 100, 300, and 500 files are admitted files, including files subsequently scrubbed or reduced; they are not all successful payouts. Conservative loses $10,000 of potential fees to eligibility scrubs and $5,000 to fee reductions or reversals, leaving $60,000 recognized fees. Base loses $30,000 and $15,000, leaving $255,000. Scaled loses $30,000 and $20,000, leaving $450,000. Average realized fees per admitted file are consequently $600, $850, and $900. Record a reason code for every loss: wrong owner, unsupported succession, duplicate filing, contractual defect, payout reduction, or uncollectible authorized invoice. Do not mechanically label all these events bad debt. A file rejected before a fee becomes recognizable is pipeline attrition; a later receivable loss has a different accounting treatment. QuickBooks or Xero should receive only the amounts supported by the recognition policy, with the operational bridge maintained in SQLite or a controlled spreadsheet. A weekly reconciliation must connect property records, executed agreements, administrator notices, invoices, and cash receipts without converting optimistic search values into sales. Count reopened files separately so a resubmission cannot manufacture apparent acquisition productivity.

The twelve mapped plays below are chapter-level operating buckets, not twelve independently additive revenue forecasts. The supplied TRACK_1 play, b2b_class_action_contingency_recovery, is economically distinct from treasury finder work. Monitor court-approved administrator notices for payment-card interchange, freight, auto parts, commercial insurance, and SaaS settlements, including large corporate antitrust funds. Treat the proposed 85–90% small-business nonfiling rate as a sourcing hypothesis until the specific administrator supplies defensible participation data. A settlement fund's headline size does not establish an individual business's allocation. For an illustrative $20,000 verified payout, a permitted 30% contingency generates $6,000 potential fees; a $600 reduction allowance leaves $5,400. Delivery of $2,400, acquisition of $900, systems allocation of $300, and collection support of $600 leave $1,200 contribution before shared overhead. The proposed 25–33% range is usable only where the contract, applicable law, and settlement procedures permit it. Fall back to verified operating businesses with primary processor or vendor statements and court-approved third-party claim-filing riders where required. Never invent transactions, beneficial ownership, or purchase history to improve the payout formula. Keep this example outside the canonical annual totals unless it replaces an explicitly budgeted cohort.

callout.title: Protect the Denominator Before Optimizing the Funnel
callout.body: Recovery businesses lose margin when search matches masquerade as qualified, collectible files.
items: Quote against the documented recoverable amount, not an aggregated search result containing duplicate properties or similarly named owners.
Ask corporate prospects for one primary processor, vendor, or treasury record before commissioning an expensive historical document search.
Track client-receipt-to-fee-payment time separately from treasury processing time; faster document work cannot cure an owner's unpaid invoice.
Reuse a verified corporate authority packet only after checking current officers, successor rights, property identifiers, and jurisdiction-specific requirements.

sections.heading: 2. Reconcile Every Deduction to the Canonical Owner Profit
paragraphs: The annual waterfall below reconciles exactly to the scorecard, but its intermediate cost allocations are explicit planning assumptions rather than reported operating history. Begin with the prospective fee pool, subtract eligibility scrubs, subtract fee reductions and reversals, and arrive at recognized service revenue. Then deduct delivery labor, acquisition, systems, administration, and financing plus collection expense. Conservative costs total $45,000, Base $159,375, and Scaled $225,000. Subtracting those amounts from $60,000, $255,000, and $450,000 yields owner profit of $15,000, $95,625, and $225,000, respectively. Dividing profit by recognized revenue produces exactly 25%, 37.5%, and 50%. Do not divide profit by underlying property recovered or by the unreduced prospective fee pool. Likewise, do not deduct the same reversal twice through both the fee bridge and an operating expense account. Maintain an accounting-policy crosswalk for presentation differences without changing the economic total. The scorecard's owner profit is treated here as the owner's operating residual before personal income taxes; an additional hypothetical owner salary has not been silently deducted. Entity-level tax treatment and compensation structure require separate budget decisions.

Delivery labor must purchase completed, auditable work rather than contractor availability. Conservative allocates $18,000 across 100 admitted files, or $180 each; Base allocates $65,000 across 300, or $216.67; Scaled allocates $100,000 across 500, or $200. Base's higher unit delivery cost represents a harder document mix, not a calculation error. Use fixed work packages for identity verification, corporate authority assembly, claim preparation, and exception handling, with rework ownership written into the engagement. Contractor classification follows the actual relationship, not the spreadsheet label. The 1 FT + 2 C Conservative and Base structures assume the owner is the full-time operator and contractors supply variable delivery capacity. Scaled's 2 FT + 3 C includes an additional employee whose loaded cost must fit inside the delivery and administration allocations. Two contractors do not imply two full-time salaries. Model hours and accepted deliverables explicitly. At an illustrative $40 blended delivery hour, $18,000 buys 450 hours, $65,000 buys 1,625, and $100,000 buys 2,500. Any employee benefits, payroll taxes, or contractor rework consuming that budget reduce the remaining production hours and must appear in capacity planning.

Acquisition budgets are $6,000, $40,000, and $55,000, equivalent to $60, $133.33, and $110 per admitted file. These denominators include later scrubs, preventing the marketing report from hiding failed files. Count purchased data, mail, calling labor, referral payments where permitted, and campaign software once, assigning shared subscriptions consistently between acquisition and systems. Systems plus administration equal $18,000, $38,000, and $50,000 annually, or $1,500, $3,166.67, and $4,166.67 monthly. Those fixed-overhead assumptions fit the supplied $1,500–$8,000 monthly opex planning range; all-in monthly expense is higher once variable delivery, acquisition, and collection costs are included. Financing and collection budgets of $3,000, $16,375, and $20,000 include expected interest, payment charges, and external collection support, not an unexplained balancing reserve. Replace each component with actual vendor quotes before spending. A prudent cash reserve is retained liquidity, not automatically an expense. Client distrust increases both CAC and invoice delays, so state plainly that owners can claim directly without hiring the service. Test plain-language letters against aggressive recovery language using admitted-file economics, not response rates alone, and retain dated campaign evidence.

sections.heading: 3. Fund the Claim Clock and the Invoice Clock Separately
paragraphs: Cash conversion starts when the operator funds acquisition or document work, not when the treasury acknowledges a claim. Track four dates: initial cash outlay, complete submission, owner receipt of property, and operator receipt of fees. Treasury review and settlement distribution delays occur before the owner has cash; invoice DSO measures the subsequent receivable interval under the contract. A court distribution hold, missing indemnity, or returned treasury check can extend the first interval without changing DSO at all. For planning, Conservative assumes 150 days before owner receipt plus 30 days to collect fees, Base 120 plus 30, and Scaled 90 plus 30. These 180-, 150-, and 120-day cash-outlay-to-fee intervals are assumptions, not published treasury service commitments. An accepted submission is neither a payable invoice nor a bankable receivable unless the agreement and applicable accounting policy support that conclusion. Record each jurisdiction's observed median and slow-tail duration separately. Do not finance a slow estate file with the average timing of simple corporate cash claims. Review status through official portals and administrator correspondence; automation should surface exceptions, not repeatedly submit duplicate claims that restart manual review or confuse ownership evidence.

A first-pass float budget multiplies monthly cash operating expense by the modeled funding interval. Using annual costs divided by twelve gives $3,750 for Conservative, $13,281.25 for Base, and $18,750 for Scaled. Six, five, and four months of those costs require $22,500, $66,406.25, and $75,000 respectively before a contingency cushion. Adding 15% produces $25,875, $76,367.19, and $86,250. This is a conservative steady-spending approximation, not an exact receivables formula: some costs occur late, some contractor payments can be milestone-based, and mature cohorts generate overlapping receipts. Build a weekly cash schedule to locate the actual trough before committing funding. The supplied $5,000–$35,000 startup capital range can support the illustrated Conservative float only toward its upper end and before additional launch costs. It does not independently fund the illustrated Base or Scaled pipeline. Those cases require retained cash, staged starts, or committed external capital. Time to first deal of 3–12 months must also be distinguished from time to first collected fee. A twelve-month zero-receipt ramp at Conservative spending consumes $45,000 before launch costs, exceeding the stated startup range.

Treat client assets as unavailable working capital even when a payment arrangement permits some administrative involvement. Prefer treasury or administrator payment directly to the verified owner, followed by a clearly authorized service invoice. Never divert property to cover unrelated payroll. For the settlement example, $4,200 of delivery, acquisition, systems, and collection spending could precede fee receipt; a 270-day distribution interval plus 30-day collection interval requires carrying that exposure for roughly ten months. Collection support may actually be paid later, so the weekly schedule should replace this deliberately conservative upper-bound treatment. At an illustrative 12% simple annual borrowing rate, carrying $4,200 for ten months costs $420 before lender fees, reducing the example's $1,200 contribution to $780 if financing was not already allocated. Avoid double counting when borrowing costs are inside the annual financing line. A lender's advance against a disputed or nonassignable claim may be unavailable regardless of expected payout. Negotiate contractor milestones around accepted evidence packages rather than making payment depend entirely on uncontrollable treasury decisions. Release cash cushions only after cohort loss experience, aging, and actual receipts support the release, not because the profit statement looks strong.

callout.title: Verify Four Conditions Before Funding the Next Cohort
callout.body: A profitable forecast cannot authorize an invalid contract or pay contractors during a distribution hold.
items: Verify finder registration, contracting restrictions, fee limits, required disclosures, and claimant authority for every jurisdiction represented in the cohort.
Verify that all modeled recoveries belong to the identified owner and that every settlement claim is supported by primary transaction records.
Verify committed unrestricted cash covers the weekly projected trough, a ninety-day delay scenario, and separately budgeted launch costs.
Verify invoice triggers, payment destinations, fee-recognition treatment, reversal handling, and the owner's direct-claim option before outreach or signing.

sections.heading: 4. Stress the Cohort Before Scaling Matching and Status Automation
paragraphs: Stress the fee pool, not just the margin percentage. A five-percentage-point increase in combined scrub and reversal losses removes $3,750 from Conservative revenue, $15,000 from Base, and $25,000 from Scaled because the underlying prospective pools are $75,000, $300,000, and $500,000. Holding costs fixed, owner profits fall to $11,250, $80,625, and $200,000. A separate 25% CAC increase adds $1,500, $10,000, and $13,750 of cost, leaving $13,500, $85,625, and $211,250. A separate 20% delivery increase adds $3,600, $13,000, and $20,000, leaving $11,400, $82,625, and $205,000. Combined, all three shocks leave $6,150, $57,625, and $166,250. These are sensitivities around the canonical cases, not replacements for their published profits. They deliberately hold throughput and other costs constant to expose first-order vulnerability. A real downturn can also lower close rates, delay collections, and increase borrowing expense simultaneously. Run that correlated downside in the weekly cash model rather than pretending independent stress columns describe the worst possible outcome. Preserve a dated assumption register so later performance comparisons cannot rewrite the original investment decision or hide deteriorating cohort quality.

Set acquisition ceilings from contribution after expected losses, not from the face value of found property. Conservative's $600 realized fee minus $180 delivery leaves $420 before CAC, systems, administration, and collection costs. Base leaves approximately $633.33 after its $216.67 delivery cost; Scaled leaves $700 after $200 delivery. Under the allocated annual model, the remaining non-acquisition costs per admitted file are $210, $181.25, and $140. Therefore the zero-profit acquisition ceilings are $210, approximately $452.08, and $560 per admitted file. Those are break-even limits, not recommended bids. Current acquisition spending leaves the canonical per-file profits of $150, $318.75, and $450. If one admitted file requires ten qualified responses, Conservative's $60 admitted-file CAC permits only $6 per qualified response before additional intake costs. Record matching should improve verified admission efficiency, while claim-status tracking should reduce manual touches and prevent stale packets. Neither automation lever increases the lawful fee cap or creates entitlement to property. Measure duplicate rate, false-owner matches, contractor minutes, missing-document loops, and cash realization by acquisition vintage before increasing campaign volume. Stop paid intake when incremental files consume contribution or exceed verified document-handling capacity.

Operational controls must preserve both economic evidence and claimant trust. California Code of Civil Procedure section 1582 addresses covered finder agreements and their fee ceiling; New York Abandoned Property Law section 1416 addresses recovery agreements, including its 15% compensation limit. Florida Statutes section 717.135 specifies requirements for covered recovery or purchase agreements, including disclosures and compensation provisions. Apply the current text to the actual transaction rather than copying a national contract template. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(e) governs settlement approval in covered class actions, but the settlement agreement, court orders, and administrator instructions determine the operational filing requirements. Maintain a restricted evidence repository for identity documents and bank information, with role-based access, encrypted storage, and documented retention periods. California Civil Code section 1798.81.5 supplies a concrete reasonable-security requirement for covered personal information. Keep raw identity documents out of broad-access Airtable views and campaign exports. Publish a monthly operating pack with cohort revenue, losses by cause, admitted-file CAC, delivery hours, aging, and unrestricted cash. The scaling decision should follow collected-fee quality and staffing capacity, not the number of attractive treasury records harvested by an automated matcher or the headline size of settlement funds.

chapters.pull_quote: Found property is a lead, an approved claim is a milestone, and only a collected lawful fee can fund the next cohort.
action_checklist: Build a fee-only cohort ledger linking every admitted file to owner authority, property identifiers, applicable contract rules, and expected fee timing.
Reconcile prospective fees through scrubs and reversals to exactly $60,000, $255,000, and $450,000 of canonical recognized annual revenue.
Allocate delivery, acquisition, systems, administration, and collection costs to reproduce $15,000, $95,625, and $225,000 annual owner profit.
Construct a weekly cash schedule separating treasury processing, payout restrictions, invoice DSO, launch costs, and unrestricted funding commitments.
Test five-point attrition, twenty-five-percent CAC, twenty-percent labor, and ninety-day payout-delay shocks before expanding paid acquisition.
Verify state finder requirements and settlement-specific filing authority, disclose direct claiming, and protect identity evidence before admitting new files.

chapters.question_prompt: How do you allocate startup capital ($5,000–$35,000 USD) and configure a lean, low-opex ($1,500–$8,000 USD/mo) production stack without wasting cash on bloated overhead?
chapters.title: Startup Capital, Lean Infrastructure & Pre-Flight Stack
chapters.subtitle: Treasury Ledger Intake, Corporate Warrant Matching, State Finder-Fee Controls, and a Reserve-First Production Stack
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #5, Unclaimed Property Recovery, holds Rank #04 with an 89/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. This chapter builds the capital and infrastructure foundation supporting the volume's 12 mapped plays, concentrating on state treasury escheatment and corporate warrant recovery. Preserve at least half of startup cash for operating runway; buy identity evidence, secure document handling, and jurisdiction-specific contracts before buying prospecting volume. Recognized service fees, never recovered client principal, anchor the scorecard: Conservative produces $15,000 annual owner net profit, Base produces $95,625, and Scaled produces $225,000. A twelve-layer stack separates free matching utilities from conditional paid services. Reserve arithmetic, lawful fee ceilings, corporate authority checks, and a complete practice claim determine readiness more reliably than an expensive office or oversized software subscription.

sections.heading: 1. Fund the collection delay before funding the workstation
paragraphs: Start with a cash envelope, not a subscription list. The authorized startup range is $5,000–$35,000, while the first deal may take 3–12 months; neither fact establishes when the first service fee will clear. Separate formation spending, recoverable operating runway, and client principal in both the budget and bank records. The allocation below preserves $2,500 of a $5,000 launch, $12,000 of a $20,000 launch, and $21,000 of a $35,000 launch as working capital. Those reserves represent 50%, 60%, and 60% of starting cash. They are operating reserves, not money for advancing a claimant's expected distribution. At $1,500 monthly fixed overhead, the smallest reserve funds only 1.67 months, the middle reserve funds eight months, and the largest funds fourteen months. Therefore the $5,000 version is a constrained validation launch requiring separate earned income or additional committed funding before sustained production. Do not describe that envelope as a fully funded twelve-month business. Preserve the reserve in a separate business savings account, reconcile transfers weekly, and require a written case-level justification before consuming it for evidence purchases. Unspent setup allocations stay in cash rather than becoming permission to upgrade equipment.

Use the seven allocation categories as spending ceilings, not vendor quotations. Formation includes state filing charges, registered agent needs, and bookkeeping setup; obtain the actual state schedule before committing the amount. Legal configuration buys review of finder eligibility, contract timing, fee limits, and corporate signatory authority for the initial jurisdiction. It does not buy nationwide coverage. The equipment allowance assumes an existing usable computer at the smallest tier and encrypted replacement hardware only where necessary. Security setup includes authentication keys and recovery preparation rather than a decorative monitoring dashboard. Outreach funds a narrow batch of verified corporate contacts; evidence funds certified records, postage, and permitted document retrieval. When a jurisdiction requires registration, a bond, or insurance exceeding the envelope, reallocate discretionary setup cash or postpone that jurisdiction without reducing the reserve below half of starting capital. Review errors-and-omissions and cyber coverage for social engineering, identity-document handling, contractor acts, and any exclusion affecting recovery services. Request written coverage explanations rather than relying on a generic business-policy label. A home office and scheduled contractor hours are usually more useful here than leased premises, dedicated sales seats, or prepaid enterprise data.

Reconcile the operating plan to the canonical scorecard before setting a hiring budget. Conservative revenue of $60,000 less $45,000 total modeled costs yields $15,000 owner net profit. Base revenue of $255,000 less $159,375 costs yields $95,625. Scaled revenue of $450,000 less $225,000 costs yields $225,000. These are annual recognized service fees and annual owner profit, not recovered asset balances or monthly cash collections. For an illustrative cost bridge, assign fixed monthly overhead of $1,500, $3,500, and $8,000 respectively. Annual fixed costs then equal $18,000, $42,000, and $96,000, leaving $27,000, $117,375, and $129,000 for all remaining modeled costs. Those residuals are budget capacity, not permission to exclude labor or duplicate contractor charges. Keep 1 FT + 2 C in the first two cases and 2 FT + 3 C in Scaled; contractor counts do not imply full-time salaries. Record actual hours and payment terms. At $8,000 monthly overhead, even the $21,000 reserve lasts only 2.625 months before variable spending. Delay that burn rate until collected fees or additional committed capital support it. An unsigned prospect list contributes nothing to available runway.
