sections.heading: 3. Instrument the desk against the canonical fee economics
paragraphs: Anchor every dashboard to recognized service fees, not the face value of property discovered or money returned to owners. The canonical Conservative case is $60,000 revenue, $45,000 implied total expense, and $15,000 owner net profit at 25%. Base is $255,000 revenue, $159,375 expense, and $95,625 profit at 37.5%. Scaled is $450,000 revenue, $225,000 expense, and $225,000 profit at 50%. Conservative and Base each use one full-time person plus two contractors; Scaled uses two full-time people plus three contractors. These are annual scorecard outcomes, not promises that this month's leads will produce next month's collections. The $1,500–$8,000 monthly operating-spend range does not replace the scenario's total implied expense envelope; staffing, variable processing, and other modeled costs must reconcile inside that envelope. Budget $5,000–$35,000 startup capital separately and plan for three to twelve months before the first deal. A source subscription that accelerates discovery but not document acceptance may deepen the cash trough. Track committed spend and expected collection dates weekly so delayed claims do not force premature fee invoices or careless acceptance of weak matches.

Use an explicitly illustrative ten-percent fee only where the applicable state rules, waiting period, registration, contract form, and property category permit it. At that rate, the Conservative revenue corresponds to $600,000 recovered client assets, Base to $2,550,000, and Scaled to $4,500,000. Those principal amounts stay outside recognized desk revenue. If an average successful claim produces $2,000 of collectible fees, the Conservative case requires thirty successes annually; Base can comprise 127 successes at $2,000 plus one at $1,000; Scaled requires 225 successes at $2,000. These decompositions explain arithmetic without asserting a universal claim-size distribution. For prospect screening, a $10,000 property with a permitted ten-percent fee and a twenty-percent probability of collectible success yields $200 expected fees. Subtract $70 research, $40 documentation, and $15 communication to leave $75 before fixed overhead and delay costs. If the property is only $1,000, the same probability produces $20 expected fees and fails that cost screen. Batch related claims with shared authority documents where the custodian permits it, but never combine owners or omit property-specific evidence merely to improve apparent unit economics.

Make pipeline diagnostics explain lost time rather than decorate a dashboard. Use SQLite integrity checks, foreign-key enforcement, unique property constraints, and unittest fixtures for parser regressions. A saved HTML example should demonstrate what happens when a portal returns a maintenance page instead of search results. Test missing amount fields, multiple owner rows, punctuation changes, and withdrawn records without silently converting absence into zero value. Structured logs should record source, batch, parser version, response status, elapsed time, and retry count while excluding claimant identifiers and document contents. Honor Retry-After where supplied, use bounded exponential backoff, and stop repeatedly failing jobs instead of hammering a source. Alert on abrupt count changes, stale active claims, duplicate submissions, and fees without supporting recovery evidence. Separate submitted, accepted, paid-to-owner, invoiced, collected, and recognized-fee milestones; cash collection and revenue recognition may occur on different dates. Reconcile the fee ledger to payment records and the accounting ledger monthly. The owner reviews exceptions while contractors process documented research tasks. This division protects the small-team model because automation reduces repetitive observation without delegating disputed ownership or payment authority to a matching score.

sections.heading: 4. Qualify the transferable-credit adjacency without confusing leads, credits, and fees
paragraphs: The specified adjacent play is transferable_tax_credit_brokerage_syndication, Transferable Federal & State Tax Credit Brokerage & Syndication (IRA § 6418 / Film / Historic), TRACK_1. Reuse the desk's provenance and entity-resolution capabilities, not its unclaimed-property fee assumptions. DOE and EPA publications can identify projects, developers, and contaminated-land opportunities, but there is no single universal DOE/EPA interconnection queue that establishes transferable credits. Actual queue research belongs with ISO, RTO, and utility sources such as PJM; queue position does not prove construction, placed-in-service status, credit amount, or tax eligibility. Georgia and Louisiana film offices, state revenue agencies, and historic preservation programs provide separate lead channels whose certification and transfer rules must be examined individually. Federal historic rehabilitation credits under IRC § 47 are not automatically transferable under § 6418. State historic and brownfield programs may have their own transfer mechanics. Record the exact credit statute, issuing authority, project entity, tax year, certification stage, and buyer-use constraints before soliciting offers. When the public record cannot establish eligibility, request seller documentation or discard the lead instead of converting a project listing into an asserted tax asset.

The supplied commercial spread assumes origination at $0.82–$0.88 per dollar of credit and placement at $0.92–$0.96. On $1,000,000 face value, those ranges imply $820,000–$880,000 seller proceeds and $920,000–$960,000 buyer outlay, with a paired gross spread of $40,000–$140,000 before insurance, diligence, escrow, and intermediary costs. At $0.85 and $0.94, the illustrative spread is $90,000. These are supplied pricing assumptions, not current market quotations or automatically recognized broker revenue. Crucially, IRC § 6418(e)(2) prevents a transferee from making a subsequent transfer election for the acquired credit. Therefore, do not implement the federal workflow as the desk buying a credit and reselling it. Structure a direct eligible transfer between the originating taxpayer and eligible unrelated buyer, with separately documented intermediary compensation and transaction expenses. A buyer-funded escrow can coordinate that direct transfer and disbursements without making the desk an intermediate credit owner. Corporate and high-net-worth buyers still require tax-capacity analysis; passive-activity restrictions can materially constrain an individual's ability to use purchased credits. For state credits, verify whether resale is permitted rather than importing federal mechanics or pricing.

The risk fallback is strict: never hold unhedged credit inventory or advance the seller's proceeds from the recovery desk's operating cash. Require buyer-funded escrow, synchronized document delivery, and non-cancelable tax-credit insurance as the specified play's execution condition, while examining the actual policy's exclusions, limits, retention, representations, and claim procedures. Non-cancelable wording does not erase fraud exclusions or establish coverage for every recapture event. If suitable coverage or an eligible funded buyer cannot be secured, decline execution or remain a disclosed origination-only intermediary without principal exposure. For federal credits, verify required pre-filing registration, transfer-election documentation, cash consideration, and the seller's supporting credit calculation under the applicable regulations. Keep credit face value, seller proceeds, buyer outlay, escrow balances, and earned intermediary compensation in distinct ledger fields. None of this illustrative adjacency changes Volume 007's $60,000, $255,000, and $450,000 canonical service-revenue cases. Launch it only with separate workflow ownership and transaction expertise. The transferable skill is disciplined evidence handling; the dangerous assumption is that finding a public project creates a freely tradable asset or an immediately collectible brokerage fee.

sections.heading: 1. Classify the asset before choosing the state contract
paragraphs: Begin every file with asset classification, not a nationwide finder agreement. Record the property identifier, reporting holder, custodial state, apparent owner, owner address history, asset type, and actual reporting or delivery dates available from the custodian. A corporate uncashed warrant still held by an issuing agency may follow that agency's reissuance procedure rather than the state treasury's finder statute. An estate claim requires authority from an executor, administrator, or qualifying successor; a dissolved company's claim requires a supported chain of corporate authority. California Code of Civil Procedure section 1582 addresses recovery agreements, including a restricted contracting interval and a ten-percent compensation ceiling. New York Abandoned Property Law section 1416 imposes its own agreement requirements and fifteen-percent ceiling. Neither number is a national default. Determine the governing provision, its current text, the relevant property category, and the event that starts each waiting period before presenting terms. If a required date cannot be established, move the record into a research queue and do not seek a signature. A promising balance cannot repair an agreement executed during a prohibited interval. Store the source document and reviewer decision alongside the eligibility calculation so another operator can reproduce the conclusion.

Build a versioned jurisdiction register with separate fields for finder registration, occupational licensing, bonds, required disclosures, permitted compensation, expense treatment, cancellation rights, and authorization format. Florida Statutes section 717.135 supplies recovery-agreement requirements, while section 717.1400 addresses registration of specified professional categories participating in claims representation. Read those provisions together with the Department of Financial Services' current instructions; a business filing alone does not establish eligibility to represent claimants. Investigative work can introduce another boundary: California Business and Professions Code section 7539 defines private investigation activities, subject to statutory exceptions. Determine whether the actual locating and investigative services require a licensed provider before selling them. Ordinary document collection also differs from representing an estate in a contested proceeding or advising a creditor about litigation strategy. Route disputed heirship, adverse ownership claims, and contested court appearances to appropriately authorized counsel. Use a separate engagement and identify who pays for that work. Review the register before entering a new state, changing a contract, or expanding a service. Archive the effective date and official source rather than relying on an aggregator's summary. Disable affected templates when a rule changes; training alone will not prevent staff from reusing obsolete documents.

Identity evidence should prove entitlement without becoming a reusable identity dossier. Collect the claimant's relationship to the named owner first, then request only the documents required for that relationship and custodian. An old address match can support research but cannot establish current signing authority. A corporate file should connect the reported name to the present entity through incorporation records, merger documents, assumed-name filings, and an authorized signer. Use a restricted Microsoft SharePoint library or equivalent controlled repository for sensitive records, with multifactor authentication, role-based access, and an access log. A CRM should hold document status and links rather than full identity scans. California Civil Code section 1798.81.5 establishes reasonable-security duties for covered personal information; section 1798.82 addresses breach notification when its conditions apply. Federal Trade Commission Act section 5 also matters when privacy promises or security representations are deceptive or unfair. Other privacy regimes depend on business thresholds, data categories, and location, so assess applicability rather than claiming universal coverage. Establish retention periods by document class, required records, disputes, and litigation holds. Give contractors only their assigned files, prohibit local downloads where practical, and revoke access when assignments end. Preserve decision evidence without keeping unnecessary identity material indefinitely.

callout.title: Four checks before the first recovery agreement
callout.body: A record advances only when another reviewer can reproduce its asset classification, authority determination, timing, and fee calculation.
items: Confirm the custodian and property category; distinguish treasury property from issuer-held warrants and bankruptcy claims.

sections.heading: 2. Price the service and make every contract trigger observable
paragraphs: The contract should name the legal provider, claimant, custodian, identified property, and precise service scope. Describe record research, document organization, status tracking, and submission assistance only to the extent the provider may perform them. State prominently: 'You may claim this property directly from the government custodian without hiring or paying our service. Our fee purchases optional assistance, not access to a government benefit.' Use any additional state-required wording without dilution. Define the fee base as the specified property actually recovered, subject to the applicable statute, rather than every future asset discovered under the owner's name. Define when a fee is earned and when payment becomes due; a portal status change is not the same event as cleared proceeds. Prefer payment to the owner followed by a transparent invoice, unless the custodian authorizes another lawful mechanism. Do not add processing charges that defeat a compensation ceiling. Include required cancellation mechanics and a plain description of what happens when the custodian denies a claim. A narrow authorization should identify permitted communications and submissions. It should not silently authorize endorsing checks, changing payment destinations, settling disputes, or transferring ownership. Have the signer receive the completed agreement and every incorporated fee schedule.

Treat anti-circumvention language as attribution protection, not ownership of the claimant's relationship with the state. Identify the property and documented work that could support an earned fee under applicable law. A direct filing, required cancellation right, or unrelated recovery must not become an automatic penalty. Avoid perpetual exclusivity, multiples of the expected fee, and clauses demanding compensation before a legally permitted trigger. A liability limitation should address ordinary service errors with a reasonable negotiated allocation while preserving nonwaivable rights and identifying exclusions appropriate to fraud, intentional misconduct, and sensitive-data incidents. State which forum and governing law apply, but do not assume a chosen state displaces mandatory protections elsewhere. Explain mediation, court access, arbitration if used, cost allocation, and any small-claims carveout in readable terms. For data ownership, distinguish the owner's documents and claim evidence from the operator's preexisting templates and internal matching methods. Give the owner usable copies of their file and define retention and deletion responsibilities. Prohibit contractors from reselling lead lists or using identity evidence for unrelated work. Public availability of a property listing does not create permission to commercialize every document subsequently collected. Have local counsel review the actual template and service model, not merely a generic engagement letter.

Keep service economics separate from recovered principal in every proposal and ledger. For a simple planning model, assume a lawful ten-percent fee and an average completed recovery of $10,000. Each paid completion generates $1,000 of recognized service revenue, not $10,000. Sixty completions produce the Conservative $60,000 revenue case; 255 produce Base revenue of $255,000; 450 produce Scaled revenue of $450,000. Their underlying client recoveries are $600,000, $2,550,000, and $4,500,000 respectively. Those recovery totals are illustrative throughput assumptions, not extra income. The canonical owner-profit cases remain $15,000 at 25%, $95,625 at 37.5%, and $225,000 at 50%, implying total annual costs of $45,000, $159,375, and $225,000. Conservative and Base staffing is one full-time operator plus two contractors; Scaled uses two full-time staff plus three contractors. Do not assume every jurisdiction permits this example fee or that every signed file pays. A $1,200 recovery produces only $120 at ten percent; two hours costing $45 each plus $20 of verification expense leave $10 before overhead. Offer the direct-claim route instead of absorbing structurally uneconomic work. Track earned, invoiced, collected, disputed, and written-off fees separately. Treasury processing delays affect working capital even when the expected fee remains collectible.

callout.title: Protect the fee by reducing ambiguity before submission
callout.body: Experienced recovery operators preserve evidence of what was authorized, what was recovered, and why the resulting invoice is correct.

sections.heading: 3. Use outreach that survives owner skepticism and channel rules
paragraphs: Separate the legality of finding a record from permission to contact a person through a particular channel. A public treasury listing does not supply consent for automated marketing texts. The Telephone Consumer Protection Act, 47 U.S.C. section 227, and 47 CFR section 64.1200 impose requirements that depend on technology, destination, content, consent, and applicable exemptions. Document those facts before using a dialer, prerecorded voice, or text platform. Screen applicable telephone campaigns against national and company-specific do-not-call requirements, observe permitted calling hours, and evaluate state restrictions separately. A manually dialed call does not erase other telemarketing duties. Commercial email must satisfy CAN-SPAM requirements under 15 U.S.C. section 7704, including truthful routing and subject information, required identification, a valid postal address, and a working opt-out mechanism. Honor opt-outs within the statutory period and prevent later lead imports from restoring suppressed recipients. Use a central suppression table across staff, contractors, and vendors. Before recording discovery calls, assess applicable recording-consent law and obtain the required permission; notes are a practical alternative when recording is unnecessary. Vendor settings and a purchased contact list are inputs, not evidence that a campaign is permitted. Preserve the screening result and script version with each outreach batch.

Use this first-contact letter verbatim after adding the provider's actual identity, postal address, and official custodian address in the letterhead: 'We are a private recovery service, not a government agency. A public unclaimed-property record may relate to you or your business; a name match alone does not establish ownership. You can search and claim directly through the government custodian without paying us. If you prefer optional assistance, we can explain our services and any permitted fee before you decide. Please do not send identity documents, bank information, or your Social Security number in response to this letter. You may independently locate the custodian's official website and contact details. To stop future contact from us, reply with stop or use the contact method printed above.' For email, add the functioning unsubscribe mechanism and required commercial identification; the script is content, not a replacement for channel controls. Do not print a full property value, former home address, or identity clue on the envelope. Avoid treasury-style seals, official-looking case numbers, fabricated deadlines, and statements that funds will disappear unless the recipient hires you. A clean letter may convert fewer impulsive replies while producing better-informed clients and fewer disputed signatures.

After the recipient agrees to discuss the service, use this discovery opening: 'Before we discuss documents, are you the named owner or someone authorized to act for that owner? Please describe your relationship without giving account numbers or identity-document details. We will explain the evidence the custodian requires and provide a secure submission method if you choose our service. You can also claim directly without us. Would you like the official direct-claim instructions first?' For a corporation, continue: 'What is the current legal entity name, and who can authorize this engagement? Has the reported business merged, dissolved, or changed names?' For fees, say: 'Our written agreement identifies the property, the permitted fee calculation, and when payment becomes due. We will not ask you to sign until those terms and your authority are clear.' If the person declines, say: 'Understood. We will record your request and stop further marketing contact through the channels you identify.' Do not turn that exchange into another sales pitch. Log dispositions without speculative comments about age, vulnerability, or wealth. Measure verified-owner conversations, signed eligible files, completed recoveries, and paid fees separately. High response rates are meaningless when identity mismatch or unsupported authority prevents a valid submission.

sections.heading: 4. Keep bankruptcy claim purchases on a separate underwriting rail
paragraphs: The mapped play chapter11_trade_claim_convenience_class_rollup belongs to TRACK_1 and requires a different legal and economic model from treasury recovery. It purchases documented small trade claims below risk-adjusted expected plan distributions. The seller transfers a claim rather than hiring a finder to recover state-held property. Use PACER and the court-designated claims agent to examine the petition, Schedule E/F, claims register, bar-date orders, disclosure statement, proposed or confirmed plan, and claim-objection docket. Schedule E/F is a research source, not conclusive evidence of an allowed claim or its current owner. Under 11 U.S.C. section 1111(a), a scheduled claim may be deemed filed, subject to the exception for claims scheduled as disputed, contingent, or unliquidated; Bankruptcy Rule 3003 supplies additional filing requirements in Chapter 11. Match invoices, delivery evidence, credits, debtor entities, and proof-of-claim records before pricing. Section 502 governs allowance and objections, while section 1122(b) permits qualifying administrative-convenience classification. It does not promise a premium distribution to every small claim purchaser. Read the actual class definition, election deadline, reduction mechanism, related-holder language, and treatment of acquired claims. Never manufacture eligibility by assuming that splitting one invoice or aggregating multiple sellers changes the plan's enforceable classification rules.

Consider an illustrative portfolio with $100,000 face value purchased for $12,000. Assume verified plan treatment would distribute 30% of face on allowed claims, but underwriting supports only an 80% probability of that modeled allowance and payment outcome. Expected receipts are $100,000 times 30% times 80%, or $24,000. Subtract $12,000 purchase consideration and $4,000 of diligence, transfer, and servicing costs to obtain an $8,000 expected contribution before overhead, taxes, and the cost of tying up capital. This arithmetic is an expectation, not an observed collection or an assumption that every claim fails independently. Correlated debtor objections can affect the entire portfolio. If supported general-unsecured treatment instead yields 10% of face at the same 80% probability, expected receipts fall to $8,000 and contribution becomes negative $8,000 at the original purchase price. Stop affected purchases, enforce documented seller recourse where available, and price only supported general-unsecured recoveries. For a $2,000 target contribution under that fallback and unchanged $4,000 costs, maximum purchase consideration is $2,000. If sellers reject that price, pass. Do not import this portfolio's face value, proceeds, or trading spread into the volume's canonical service-fee scorecard.

Use a purchase agreement that identifies the debtor, case number, claim number when available, face amount, supporting documents, purchase price, and exactly what rights transfer. Obtain representations addressing ownership, prior assignments, payments, credits, disputes, and liens, with document delivery and further-assurance obligations. Separate recourse for a seller's breached representation from ordinary debtor insolvency risk; broad language is worthless when the seller cannot perform. Bankruptcy Rule 3001(e) provides different procedures depending on transfer timing and whether the transfer is for security. For a qualifying transfer other than for security after a proof of claim has been filed, the rule provides notice and a twenty-one-day transferor objection period. Follow the applicable procedure and court orders rather than treating a private signature as the entire transfer process. Track substitution, objections, distribution instructions, and any plan-specific election independently. Counsel should handle contested transfer or allowance proceedings and assess specialized rights, sanctions, tax, and solicitation issues when relevant. Keep purchase cash, acquired-claim accounting, and seller payments in a distinct ledger from service fees and owner recoveries. At each review, compare actual collections and remaining supported distributions with acquisition cost and unresolved objections. An attractive spreadsheet cannot override adverse docket evidence.

sections.heading: 1. Build an evidence ledger before connecting automation
paragraphs: Start with an event ledger, not a browser robot that clicks through treasury forms. Give every imported property a source jurisdiction, official property identifier, retrieval timestamp, source checksum, and permitted-use record. Python's csv, sqlite3, hashlib, and datetime modules are sufficient for a single-worker pilot: preserve the original row, create a normalized working record, and append subsequent decisions rather than overwriting history. Normalize punctuation and address components while retaining original spellings, because a dissolved corporation and its similarly named successor can have different ownership rights. Keep claimant documents in encrypted object storage with narrowly scoped access; the ledger holds document references, not copied identity numbers. Separate property, claimant, engagement, claim, and invoice entities so one owner with six properties does not become six contradictory customer profiles. A property listing establishes a research lead, not entitlement or permission to contact someone through every available channel. Route licensed bulk files and expressly permitted public downloads through ingestion adapters. Where a treasury offers only interactive access, assign a scheduled human lookup rather than bypassing access controls. Record the source restriction beside the adapter so future contractors cannot mistake technical access for permitted reuse.

Use explicit transitions: discovered, research-ready, identity-reviewed, agreement-reviewed, document-ready, submitted, evidence-requested, paid, and closed. An internal webhook announces a proposed transition; it never proves that a treasury accepted a claim. Implement receivers with Python's http.server only for a local prototype, placing production handlers behind a managed HTTPS endpoint with authentication, request-size limits, and durable queuing. Verify HMAC signatures using hmac.compare_digest, reject stale timestamps, and enforce an idempotency key combining engagement identifier, event type, and upstream event identifier. Store the event before acknowledging receipt. A worker then validates the current state, applies an allowed transition, and emits an audit entry. Duplicate payment notifications must not generate duplicate invoices or owner messages. Assume events can arrive late and out of order; a document-request event received after payment becomes an exception rather than reopening the claim automatically. The full-time operator owns exceptions and final decisions. Contractor one handles evidence research; contractor two assembles packets and checks status. Neither contractor can silently change fee rules or release claimant documents externally. Maintain a daily reconciliation between ledger states, official acknowledgments, and the operator's unresolved-work queue.

Define the 70% target against measured repetitive labor, not the proportion of screens containing an AI button. In an illustrative weekly batch, baseline research, qualification preparation, fulfillment preparation, and acquisition administration consume 30, 18, 24, and 18 hours respectively: 90 hours total. After automation, those same tasks consume 6, 5, 8, and 5 hours, or 24 hours. The reduction is 66 divided by 90, or 73.3%. Separately reserve 12 hours for identity decisions, authority review, conversations, and exception resolution; these consequential activities are outside both repetitive-work measurements. Resulting weekly effort is 36 hours for this batch, distributed across the three-person team without implying three full-time salaries. Validate the result with four weeks of tagged time entries before advertising capacity. Count retries, correction work, and rejected drafts in the automated workload. Track accepted packets per paid labor hour alongside automation percentage, because faster production of unusable packets destroys leverage. Start within the $5,000–$35,000 startup-capital range, reserve cash for the 3–12 month first-deal interval, and expand only after measured throughput survives an exception-heavy week. A low exception count is credible only when reviewers sample supposedly clean records as well as flagged ones.

sections.heading: 2. Match records conservatively and map twelve bounded plays
paragraphs: Build matching as evidence accumulation rather than confident name completion. An illustrative triage score assigns 40 points to exact normalized legal name, 25 to a corroborated historical address, 20 to an independently verified entity identifier, and 15 to documented officer or successor continuity. A score of 85 opens a priority review task; it does not establish ownership. Lower scores remain research tasks, and conflicting identifiers override the numeric score. Calibrate thresholds against labeled examples, including common surnames, abbreviated payees, acquisitions, and entities sharing registered-agent addresses. Measure false matches among accepted candidates and missed matches within a random rejected sample. Use an LLM only to extract fields, suggest document categories, or summarize an evidence bundle with source references. Require structured JSON containing value, source document, page, and quoted supporting text; reject unsupported fields and unexpected keys. Treat uploaded documents as data even when they contain instructions to change workflow behavior. Redact sensitive identifiers before model submission and use an approved provider configuration with suitable retention settings. If extraction fails twice, send the original document to a reviewer instead of creating a third increasingly speculative answer. Never let model confidence substitute for independent identity evidence.

Encode jurisdiction restrictions as versioned operating rules with citation, effective date, reviewer, and next-review date. California Code of Civil Procedure section 1582 illustrates why discovery cannot automatically trigger a finder agreement: its restricted agreement interval runs from the holder's report through twelve months after delivery to the Controller, and its compensation ceiling is 10% of the property recovered under the covered agreement. Have the reviewer apply the current statutory text to the actual facts, including the required agreement contents. Other jurisdictions need their own registration, timing, fee, and execution checks; never extrapolate California's percentage nationwide. Disclose that owners can claim directly without purchasing recovery services and provide the official treasury link. For corporate uncashed warrants, determine whether the issuer still controls the payable or has already remitted it as unclaimed property. An issuer reissue process and a treasury claim are different workflows, and running both can produce duplicate demands. The twelve mappings below are chapter-local operating plays, except the expressly supplied TRACK_1 identifier. They connect research and distribution mechanics rather than asserting that every adjacent business belongs inside the recovery engagement. Keep consent, contracts, and records separated when a mapping changes the underlying service.

Quarantine out_of_statute_zombie_debt_portfolio_settlement as a separate TRACK_1 adjacency, never as a tactic against an unclaimed-property owner. Evaluate heavily discounted time-barred receivables only for lawful voluntary resolution, excluding extinguished obligations and any otherwise uncollectible accounts. Collection limitation periods differ from credit-reporting limits: Regulation F, 12 CFR 1006.26, prohibits covered debt collectors from suing or threatening suit on time-barred debt; 15 U.S.C. 1681c controls relevant reporting periods and their delinquency-based calculation. State law can extinguish obligations or impose additional requirements, so account-level jurisdiction review precedes any contact. Illustratively, 100 eligible accounts with $100,000 face value might cost $2,000, with $800 validation expense and $600 outreach expense. Five voluntary payments of $500 produce $2,500 cash, leaving a $900 deficit against $3,400 cash outlay before overhead. Face value is neither collected cash nor recovery-service revenue; purchased-receivable accounting also needs separate treatment. Do not promise tradeline deletion, re-age delinquency, or imply payment is required to obtain treasury property. Suppress affected accounts, correct reporting, and suspend collection until counsel approves remediation whenever eligibility or reporting fails. Keep this experiment outside all three canonical recovery scenarios and reject it when its unit economics or evidence cannot support operation.

sections.heading: 3. Price automated runs and recover safely from failures
paragraphs: Price the pipeline at the accepted-output level. An illustrative run ingests 1,000 permitted records for $1 of compute and storage, normalizes them for $3, sends 100 redacted extraction requests at $0.02 each for $2, performs 40 permitted status checks for $2, and sends 60 authorized messages at $0.02 each for $1.20. Direct machine expense is $9.20. Add a 20% retry reserve of $1.84, making the budget $11.04 per run. These are planning assumptions, not vendor quotations; replace each rate with observed invoices. If 20 candidates require four minutes of contractor review at $30 hourly, review costs $40. Three packet checks at twelve minutes and $40 hourly add $24. Total run cost is therefore $75.04, or approximately $25.01 per accepted packet when all three pass. If only one packet passes, the cost is $75.04, demonstrating why cheap extraction cannot rescue weak targeting. Report machine expense, reviewer expense, accepted packets, and eventual fee receipts separately. Do not count an assembled packet as a paid recovery. Allocate unsuccessful research across the cohort rather than hiding it in a miscellaneous software account. Maintain the same denominator when comparing manual and automated processing.

Reconcile throughput to the canonical scorecard using an illustrative average recognized service fee of $750 per completed engagement. Conservative requires 80 completions for $60,000 revenue; Base requires 340 for $255,000; Scaled requires 600 for $450,000. At an illustrative lawful 10% contracted fee, each engagement represents $7,500 of recovered owner property, not $7,500 of operator revenue. Owner assets would total $600,000, $2,550,000, and $4,500,000 respectively, entirely outside recognized service-fee revenue. The canonical margins imply total annual expenses of $45,000, $159,375, and $225,000, leaving owner profits of $15,000, $95,625, and $225,000. Allocate labor, acquisition, research failures, software, insurance, and administration inside those totals; the run model is one component, not an additional profit projection. Average monthly total expenses are $3,750, $13,281.25, and $18,750. Consequently, the supplied $1,500–$8,000 monthly opex planning range cannot serve as an all-in expense ceiling for every scenario. Use the scenario-derived expense totals when budgeting these outcomes and resolve category definitions before committing cash. Preserve staffing at 1 FT + 2 C for Conservative and Base, and 2 FT + 3 C for Scaled. A software improvement does not authorize silently removing the second full-time role from the Scaled case.

Treat claim tracking as reconciliation against external evidence. Treasury systems do not universally expose APIs or webhooks, so adapters may consume authorized exports, owner-forwarded correspondence, or scheduled manual observations. Each observation records claim identifier, source timestamp, observed status, document request, and next permitted action. Never infer payment from a disappearing portal row. Use bounded exponential backoff with jitter for transient failures, respect published rate limits, and move repeated failures into a dead-letter queue with an assigned owner. After three failed attempts, stop unattended retries until the next reviewed schedule; distinguish a temporary outage from revoked access. Detect schema drift through required-field checks and a small set of known test records. A changed date format should quarantine the batch, not rewrite agreement eligibility dates. Keep daily encrypted backups and run a monthly restore exercise that reconciles event counts and document references. During an outage, contractors use a minimal manual worksheet containing identifiers, next actions, and reviewer initials. Import that worksheet with unique event keys after service returns. Customer updates should state the last verified milestone and the next action, avoiding invented treasury deadlines. Release invoices only after the engagement's contractual earning conditions and supporting recovery evidence are satisfied.

sections.heading: 4. Compound trusted distribution without outrunning review capacity
paragraphs: Build programmatic education around questions owners actually need answered: how to locate an official treasury portal, document a corporate name change, or distinguish an issuer-held warrant from escheated property. Generate page drafts from a jurisdiction rules table, then require an editor to verify citations, dates, direct-claim links, and state-specific instructions. Do not publish pages naming apparent owners or suggesting that an unverified amount belongs to them. A six-page pilot at $150 production cost per page costs $900. If it produces 30 qualified inquiries and three paid engagements, acquisition cost is $300 per engagement before ongoing maintenance. At the illustrative $750 fee, that leaves $450 before fulfillment and other expenses, not $450 profit. Attribute results through first-party landing-page parameters and engagement identifiers without embedding sensitive property details in URLs. Improve pages using aggregated missing-document patterns from completed cases, stripping identifiers before editorial use. This creates a useful loop: real operational friction improves education, better education attracts prepared owners, and prepared owners reduce packet revisions. Retire pages whose rules cannot be maintained. Traffic growth matters only when resulting engagements fit the evidence standards, review capacity, and fee economics of the operation.

Use professional referrals and narrow corporate outreach before broad automated messaging. Accountants, business attorneys, and corporate administrators often understand historical names and authorized signatories better than a scraped contact list. Give partners a generic evidence checklist and official direct-claim links; share a specific property's details only with appropriate authorization. An illustrative campaign researching 100 corporate contacts at $3 each costs $300. Eight substantive replies, four qualified engagements, and two eventual paid recoveries yield $150 acquisition cost per paid engagement, before fulfillment. Treat those conversions as a test hypothesis rather than a forecast. For commercial email, implement 15 U.S.C. 7704 requirements including accurate headers, nondeceptive subjects, required identification and address information, and a functioning opt-out that is honored within the statutory period. Do not disguise a private service as a treasury notice. Suppress declined recipients across every campaign, and retain only the minimal suppression data necessary to honor that choice. A satisfied owner may voluntarily share a generic resource link, but their recovery amount, documents, and testimonial require separate publication permission. Avoid public leaderboards, exposed claim identifiers, and referral incentives that conflict with applicable professional or finder rules.

Connect distribution to capacity through a weekly cohort dashboard. Track source records, reviewed matches, qualified owners, signed eligible agreements, accepted submissions, paid engagements, recognized fees, and attributable expense. Separate these stages by acquisition month because a 3–12 month first-deal interval makes same-month conversion ratios misleading. At Base, 340 paid engagements annually average 28.33 monthly, while Scaled averages 50; these are throughput requirements, not treasury processing promises. If an illustrative 40% of qualified engagements eventually pay, Base requires 850 qualified engagements annually, approximately 70.83 monthly. If only 20% pay, that requirement doubles to 1,700 annually. Use observed aging and conversion before buying more traffic. Set work-in-progress limits from reviewer minutes: 120 available packet-review minutes daily at twelve minutes per packet support ten reviews, not unlimited submissions. When identity exceptions or missing-document requests consume that reserve, slow acquisition instead of allowing unsafe automatic release. Reinvest only within the canonical expense envelope and keep cash runway separate from recognized profit. The distribution flywheel becomes scalable when each completed cohort improves source selection, document readiness, and trust while preserving the owner's direct-claim choice. Automate preparation aggressively; expand consequential throughput only as fast as evidence quality and staffed review permit.

chapters.question_prompt: How do you structure a lean 1 FT + 2 C (3 people) -> 2 FT + 3 C (5 people) pod, enforce weekly scorecards, and build transferable books that command a premium exit multiple (or durable cash cow)?
chapters.title: Pod Architecture, Contractor KPIs & Exit Valuation
chapters.subtitle: Treasury Claim Pods, Finder-Fee Cohorts, Contractor Evidence SLAs, Copyright Assignments & Buyer-Ready Earnings
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #5, Unclaimed Property Recovery, holds Rank #04 with an 89/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. Its 12 mapped plays become transferable only when identity evidence, finder agreements, treasury submissions, and fee collections survive the founder's absence. This chapter assigns those plays to a lean 1 FT + 2 C pod, then expands deliberately to 2 FT + 3 C. Weekly scorecards measure accepted evidence and collectible fees rather than discovered asset value. Canonical annual owner profits are $15,000 Conservative, $95,625 Base, and $225,000 Scaled. Build separate treasury cohorts, enforce concentration limits of 25% or less, secure contractor IP assignments, and normalize owner labor before discussing a sale. A premium depends on documented transferability, not a large spreadsheet of possible claims.

sections.heading: 1. Assign twelve plays to accountable seats, not twelve separate hires
paragraphs: Build the initial pod around one full-time owner-operator, one research contractor, and one evidence contractor. The owner controls client acceptance, jurisdiction selection, pricing, final submission review, and collections. The research contractor produces traceable candidate records and resolves entity aliases without deciding legal entitlement. The evidence contractor assembles owner-authorized documents, maintains status dates, and prepares submission packets without signing for claimants. The twelve-play map below is this chapter's operating allocation for Candidate #5, rather than twelve separate product lines or additional employees. It covers state-treasury escheatment, corporate uncashed warrants, and finder-fee recovery while keeping authority decisions centralized. Treat a warrant as a lead requiring classification: establish whether the issuer still handles replacement or whether the asset has entered a state's unclaimed-property process. Do not apply an escheatment workflow to an ordinary payable simply because a check is old. Every matter receives a treasury property identifier or issuer reference, an owner identifier, an evidence index, and a permitted next action. That minimum record lets either contractor continue production without inheriting the founder's memory. Keep bank instructions outside contractor-editable fields and require owner confirmation through an established contact channel before changing payment information.

At the scaled configuration, add one full-time case manager and one specialist contractor; retain the owner, researcher, and evidence contractor. The case manager owns work allocation, second-person packet review, treasury follow-up, and weekly cohort reporting. The specialist handles documented exceptions such as entity succession or probate-document coordination, with licensed counsel engaged separately when representation or legal analysis requires it. Outside advisers are purchased services, not hidden production seats counted as free capacity. Define each contractor engagement by deliverables, acceptance criteria, access limits, and negotiated service levels. Do not disguise employee-like supervision as independent contracting by changing the invoice label; federal and state classification tests still apply to the actual working relationship. Use role-based access in Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, a controlled case register in Airtable, and a document vault with access logging. Store identity documents in the vault, not in task comments or public spreadsheet links. Automate record matching and status reminders, but retain human review for identity conflicts, authority chains, and fee eligibility. The second employee earns their place by replacing owner bottlenecks and improving accepted throughput, not by introducing another layer of status meetings or duplicating contractor research.

Publish a jurisdiction card before either contractor touches a new claim class. Record finder registration requirements, agreement restrictions, fee caps, waiting periods, claimant signature requirements, and the owner's ability to claim directly without hiring the service. California Code of Civil Procedure section 1582 supplies concrete agreement restrictions, including a ten-percent compensation ceiling and a restricted contracting period; verify the applicable report and delivery dates rather than assuming every listed asset is immediately actionable. Corporate authority must connect the named property owner to the signing officer through current records, merger documents, or other accepted evidence. A matching trade name alone does not establish entitlement. Assign one reviewer to confirm that connection and a different person to check packet completeness whenever capacity permits; the owner performs the second check in the three-person pod. Reserve ten percent of planned production capacity for rejected evidence, returned mail, and treasury information requests. If exception work consumes that reserve for two consecutive weekly reviews, stop opening the affected claim class until the cause is corrected. Capacity discipline protects the canonical economics better than recruiting another contractor to process an expanding inventory of low-value, weakly matched records that cannot produce collectible service fees.

callout.title: Keep the treasury case file portable from its first day
callout.body: The most valuable operating shortcuts remove repeat investigation without weakening identity, authority, or fee controls.
items: Retain the original treasury property identifier through every alias merge so another reviewer can reconstruct the match.
Build issuer-specific warrant replacement checklists separately from state-treasury claim checklists; similar documents do not imply identical authority.
Capture the actual treasury deficiency wording in a searchable exception library, with sensitive claimant details removed.
Ask repeat corporate clients for a maintained signing-authority roster, then verify its currency before each new engagement.

sections.heading: 2. Pay for accepted evidence and enforce a weekly economic scorecard
paragraphs: Compensate contractors for accepted production rather than discovered property balances or claimant signatures. An illustrative research schedule pays $25 for a deduplicated, source-linked entity match; an evidence schedule pays $90 for a complete packet accepted against the jurisdiction checklist. A separately authorized exception task can carry an hourly ceiling, such as three hours at $45, with additional scope agreed before work continues. These are budgeting examples, not observed market rates or additions to the canonical scenario expenses. Define acceptance objectively: readable documents, complete authority links, correct property identifiers, and no unresolved identity conflict. Review delivered work within two business days, return specific defects, and pay accepted invoices on the agreed schedule. Negotiate a two-business-day correction target for in-scope contractor errors, while distinguishing new treasury requests from defects in the original deliverable. Do not shift treasury processing delays onto contractor compensation. Avoid bonuses based solely on signatures, submission count, or nominal asset value because those incentives reward weak matches and premature filing. If using a quality bonus, tie it to audited first-pass acceptance and properly documented cases, with no payment for bypassing required evidence or presenting a paid recovery service as a government office.

Hold one weekly operating review using a frozen Friday extract, with definitions that remain constant across cohorts. Track researched records, accepted identity matches, executed eligible agreements, complete packets, submissions acknowledged, treasury deficiencies, confirmed owner recoveries, recognized service fees, fee receipts, and contractor rework hours. Display both counts and denominators: first-pass packet acceptance equals accepted packets divided by packets reviewed, while recovery conversion uses a mature submission cohort rather than this week's unrelated receipts. Establish initial targets of at least ninety-five percent first-pass acceptance and zero unresolved identity conflicts at submission. Measure response time only from receipt of an actionable treasury request; stop that internal clock when the team has documented an external dependency. Report external waiting days separately instead of hiding them. Show median and ninetieth-percentile internal cycle times so a handful of neglected files cannot disappear behind an average. The owner assigns one corrective action, one accountable seat, and one due date for each breach. At scaled capacity, the case manager prepares the extract and the owner samples underlying evidence, preserving independent oversight without rebuilding every spreadsheet personally. Keep changes to metric definitions in a version log so historical improvements remain comparable.

Add unit economics to that review before increasing intake. For an illustrative cohort of twenty accepted packets, the example research and assembly rates produce $2,300 of direct contractor cost. If twelve matters ultimately generate collectible $500 fees, cohort service revenue is $6,000 and the remainder before outreach, employee labor, software, exceptions, and overhead is $3,700. That is a sensitivity example, not a replacement for the Conservative, Base, or Scaled annual scorecard. A lower lawful fee or weaker recovery rate can erase the contribution without changing packet volume. Set a minimum expected contribution threshold using jurisdiction-specific permitted fees and historical mature cohort outcomes; reject low-value work that fails it. Forecast reviewer hours as accepted packets multiplied by observed review minutes, then add measured exception time. Increase contractor assignments only when review capacity and cash reserves cover the resulting work. Monitor each client group, referral counterparty, and treasury or issuer counterparty against a twenty-five-percent concentration ceiling using trailing recognized fees and separately weighted pipeline fees. Aggregate related entities. Trigger diversification at twenty percent, and stop discretionary new concentration above twenty-five percent while honoring existing client obligations. Track cash receipts too, because delayed collections can create a liquidity concentration that revenue ratios miss.

sections.heading: 3. Reconcile fee revenue, cohort costs, and transferable operating assets
paragraphs: Keep the general ledger anchored to recognized service fees, never client property value. The Conservative case reconciles $60,000 revenue less $45,000 expenses to $15,000 owner net profit. Base reconciles $255,000 less $159,375 to $95,625. Scaled reconciles $450,000 less $225,000 to $225,000. Those expense totals are fixed consequences of the canonical margins, not discretionary targets to overwrite with attractive contractor examples. Monthly revenue equivalents are $5,000, $21,250, and $37,500, but actual receipts will be uneven because first deals can take three to twelve months. The stated $1,500–$8,000 monthly operating-expense range does not replace fully loaded annual scenario expenses; reconcile labor, variable production, and other included costs separately. Use QuickBooks Online or Xero with case identifiers on fee invoices and contractor bill lines. Record owner distributions outside operating expenses, and explain the treatment of owner wages consistently. Maintain a separate schedule for replacement owner labor because a buyer's normalized earnings calculation may differ from the chapter's owner profit presentation. Never increase the canonical profit merely by moving an ordinary production cost into an acquisition add-back. Require the monthly close to show the complete bridge from ledger accounts to each reported profit measure.

Adopt a written accrual policy with the accountant that identifies the service obligation, enforceable payment right, and treatment of contingent consideration under the applicable reporting framework. Neither a signed engagement nor a treasury acknowledgment automatically creates earned revenue. Where compensation depends on completed owner recovery, keep the expected fee in the pipeline until the contractual earning condition and recognition requirements are satisfied. Record an earned unpaid fee as a receivable only when the relevant criteria support that treatment; maintain an allowance methodology for collection risk. Contractor services already received belong in the period incurred, even if the related claim has not paid. Do not capitalize ordinary failed research simply to smooth margins. Build acquisition-month and submission-month cohort views that preserve original dates through resubmission. For each cohort, show signed eligible matters, submissions, recoveries, recognized fees, cash receipts, direct cost, and remaining exposure. Reconcile opening receivables plus earned billings less collections, credits, and write-offs to closing receivables. Keep unapplied cash and customer advances separate. If a payment arrangement temporarily brings claimant funds under the operator's control, account for the obligation separately and use the required safeguarding process; the entire deposit does not become service revenue merely because it entered a business account.

Make the operating assets transferable before a buyer requests diligence. List every contractor-created script, matching rule, checklist, template, training recording, and documentation set in an intellectual-property register. Under 17 U.S.C. section 204(a), a copyright ownership transfer generally requires a writing signed by the rights owner or authorized agent. Obtain signed assignments covering the intended deliverables, identify pre-existing materials, and secure adequate licenses for permitted embedded components. Payment alone does not establish ownership, and a contractor label does not automatically make software a work made for hire. Verify tool subscription transfer terms and source-data permissions separately; an assignment cannot transfer rights the contractor never possessed. Maintain a contract register identifying assignment restrictions, required client permissions, and whether representative authority survives a transaction. Store secrets in a controlled password manager with named accounts and a documented rotation procedure, not in the sale memorandum. Give prospective buyers aggregated cohort data first and disclose sensitive claimant records only through a restricted, purpose-limited process. Maintain retention and deletion schedules tied to actual statutory and contractual requirements. A clean transfer package demonstrates that repeatable revenue depends on owned processes and valid relationships rather than exported identity files or the founder's personal portal credentials.

callout.title: Four checks before scaling commitments or circulating a sale package
callout.body: An unresolved check pauses the affected commitment or disclosure until supporting evidence is complete.

sections.heading: 4. Value normalized earnings and choose between a sale and durable distributions
paragraphs: Discuss valuation only after defining what the buyer must replace. For a small owner-operated recovery firm, seller's discretionary earnings can be useful when the buyer will personally occupy the operating seat; an absentee buyer instead needs earnings after market-rate management and delivery labor. The canonical owner net profit figures do not automatically equal either adjusted SDE or adjusted EBITDA. Prepare separate bridges identifying recorded owner compensation, defensible personal or nonrecurring expenses, missing recurring costs, and replacement labor. Do not add back recurring lead research, normal contractor rework, or software required to keep cases moving. For discussion, use an illustrative 1.5–3.0 times adjusted SDE range for a founder-dependent book, and test 2.5–4.0 times transferable earnings only as a negotiated sensitivity for stronger operations. These are underwriting assumptions, not verified transaction comparables or interchangeable multiples on different earnings definitions. Obtain current comparable evidence before setting an asking price. A treasury receivable portfolio with unresolved identity disputes deserves different treatment from collected, repeatable corporate-client fees. The practical premium comes from low dependency, demonstrable collection quality, enforceable relationships, and controlled concentration. An attractive dashboard cannot substitute for a buyer's ability to operate the same workflow with appropriately authorized people.

A transparent sensitivity starts with the $225,000 Scaled owner profit and assumes that replacing the selling owner's remaining duties costs $90,000 annually, with no offsetting compensation add-back. Transferable earnings become $135,000; applying the illustrative 2.5–4.0 range produces $337,500–$540,000 of enterprise value. The $90,000 is a transaction-model adjustment, not a change to the canonical Scaled scenario. If replacement compensation is already fully reflected in the ledger, do not subtract it twice. The same assumed deduction leaves only $5,625 from Base profit and makes Conservative transferable earnings negative $75,000. That does not imply a negative asset price; it shows why those configurations may suit working owners better than absentee acquirers. Keep enterprise value separate from cash paid at closing. Debt, excess cash, agreed working capital, transaction expenses, taxes, seller financing, and contingent consideration affect seller proceeds. Specify whether earned fee receivables transfer and avoid counting their face value both in enterprise value and as an automatic extra payment. An earnout should define eligible pre-close cohorts, collection evidence, deductions, reporting access, dispute procedures, and buyer operating obligations. Otherwise, the headline multiple can conceal substantial collection and control risk retained by the seller.

Run a transfer drill before choosing a sale timeline. For thirty days, have the case manager route work, maintain treasury follow-ups, prepare the scorecard, and assemble the monthly close while the owner handles only documented reserved decisions. Record every interruption that requires personal knowledge, then replace that dependency with a usable instruction, valid delegation, or named relationship handoff. Repeat the drill until routine production no longer depends on private inbox history. Maintain a buyer package with at least twenty-four months of monthly results when available, mature cohort collections, concentration schedules, signed contractor agreements, and an exception register. A younger business should present its actual shorter history rather than manufacture seasoned performance. For a durable cash-cow strategy, retain the same controls and distribute only cash remaining after taxes, committed production costs, and a reserve sized to observed collection delays. Compare after-tax sale proceeds with risk-adjusted future distributions using explicit assumptions about claim availability and owner effort. Treasury inventory is finite, and historical discoveries are not subscription revenue. Renew the sourcing engine, protect client trust, and maintain diversification even when no sale is planned. The best exit option is a business the owner can keep without being trapped inside its daily evidence queue.

chapters.pull_quote: A transferable recovery book sells documented fee collection, not discovered property or the founder's memory.
action_checklist: Assign all twelve mapped plays to the three-person pod, then document the exact responsibilities moving to the scaled case manager and specialist contractor.
Issue contractor scopes with accepted-deliverable pricing, two-business-day review targets, correction terms, confidentiality duties, and signed IP assignments.
Freeze a weekly scorecard covering packet acceptance, identity exceptions, mature-cohort recovery, collectible fee economics, reviewer capacity, and contractor rework.
Aggregate related counterparties and enforce twenty-five-percent concentration ceilings across trailing fees and weighted pipeline, with early action at twenty percent.
Close the fee ledger monthly against recovery evidence, receivables, receipts, contractor accruals, and the exact three canonical annual profit cases.
Complete a thirty-day owner-dependency drill and prepare separate earnings, replacement-labor, enterprise-value, and seller-proceeds bridges before selecting a sale or distribution strategy.

chapters.title: The First 30-Day Launch Sprint & Kill / Fix / Scale Gates
chapters.subtitle: A Three-Person Treasury-Claim Sprint: Finder Restrictions, Corporate Warrant Evidence, Controlled Cash Burn, and Cohort-Based Expansion
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #5, Unclaimed Property Recovery, holds Rank #04 with an 89/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. This sprint operationalizes its 12 mapped plays through a one-full-time, two-contractor pod, concentrating on state-treasury property, corporate uncashed warrants, and lawful finder-fee engagements. Days 1–30 establish jurisdiction rules, audit identity matches, test transparent outreach, and submit evidence-complete claims. Day 30/60/90 decisions use explicit denominators, filing defects, acquisition costs, and cash reserves rather than premature collection promises. Canonical annual owner profits are $15,000 Conservative, $95,625 Base, and $225,000 Scaled; recognized service fees, never recovered client principal, fund those outcomes. With first deals typically taking 3–12 months, the initial success condition is a defensible operating system and qualified cohort, not an artificial first-month revenue target.

sections.heading: 1. Days 1–7: Bound the Jurisdiction, Assign the Pod, and Protect the Runway
paragraphs: Start with one state, one property class, and one claimant type: existing corporations seeking cash already held by a state treasury. Corporate uncashed warrants still payable by an issuing agency belong in a separate workflow until custody and the applicable recovery rules are established. The supplied mapping count is twelve; the following are sprint workstream labels, not asserted source-taxonomy names. P01 covers treasury inventory; P02 covers issuer-held warrants; P03 covers corporate claimant authority; P04 covers historical address evidence; P05 covers identity matching; P06 covers finder eligibility and fee rules; P07 covers owner outreach; P08 covers engagement execution; P09 covers evidence assembly; P10 covers claim submission; P11 covers status tracking; and P12 covers fee collection and reconciliation. Assign every record one primary play and explicit supporting plays. The full-time founder owns P06–P08 and P12, the research contractor owns P01–P05, and the claims contractor owns P09–P11. The founder retains final identity and submission decisions. Contractors receive narrow case access rather than a complete customer export. This partition makes all twelve plays observable without pretending a three-person pod can launch twelve markets simultaneously. Freeze additional jurisdictions until the first cohort clears its documented review.

On Days 1 and 2, build a rules register from the treasury's official claim instructions and current statutes. California Code of Civil Procedure §1582 addresses recovery agreements, including restricted contracting periods and a ten-percent compensation ceiling; Texas Property Code §74.507 separately governs recovery-assistance agreements and its own restrictions. Do not transplant one state's contract into another. Record the controlling section, retrieval date, restricted-period trigger, permitted fee calculation, required agreement terms, and any applicable registration requirement. Treat a missing custody date as a blocked engagement, not permission to infer that a waiting period expired. Ask the treasury to clarify ambiguous procedures without transmitting unnecessary identity documents. On Day 3, configure a case register in Airtable or a local SQLite database and a separately permissioned document repository in Google Workspace. Store treasury identifiers, evidence references, and status events in the register; keep tax identifiers and document images out of outreach exports. Enable multifactor authentication, individual accounts, access logging, and encrypted backups. Document retention and deletion rules for rejected prospects before importing records. By Day 4, a second person must reproduce five property-to-owner matches from the saved evidence alone.

Set the first-month cash-burn ceiling at $3,500: $1,500 for formation and jurisdiction-specific contract review, $750 for secure systems and records, $1,000 for contractors, and $250 for outreach. At an illustrative $50 hourly rate, the contractor allowance buys twenty combined hours, not twenty hours each. The founder supplies the remaining operating capacity without a first-month draw; personal living expenses require a separate reserve. Budget $2,500 for each of Months 2 and 3, making the ninety-day ceiling $8,500. A $32,500 starting balance leaves $24,000 after that ceiling and funds another nine months at $2,500 with $1,500 remaining. This fits the canonical $5,000–$35,000 startup range while acknowledging the 3–12-month first-deal interval. A $5,000 launch cannot support the same schedule without reduced spending or additional committed funds. Log commitments when ordered, not only when invoices clear. On Days 5–7, approve one agreement, one direct-claim disclosure, one evidence checklist, and the first twenty-record audit. No acquisition spending expands while the remaining runway falls below six months of the current maintenance budget. The $1,500–$8,000 monthly operating range describes planning capacity, not permission to exhaust available cash.

callout.title: Four Pre-Flight Checks Before Contacting an Owner
callout.body: An attractive property amount does not override an unresolved identity, custody, contracting, or cash-control defect.
items: Verify the property's present custodian and identifier; do not describe an issuer-held warrant as treasury-held property.
Document the applicable fee ceiling, restricted contracting period, agreement requirements, and registration position before offering paid recovery.
Require two independent identity links, verified corporate authority, and a second-person review of ambiguous matches.
Confirm the $3,500 first-month ceiling, six-month maintenance reserve, direct-claim disclosure, and restricted document access.

sections.heading: 2. Days 8–14: Build a Measurable Cohort and Earn Permission to Proceed
paragraphs: Days 8–10 turn the initial sample into a hundred-record research cohort. Count unique property-owner pairs, not search results, duplicate treasury pages, or multiple contacts at the same corporation. Preserve the source URL, retrieval date, displayed amount category, holder name, and property identifier. A treasury's amount band is not a verified recoverable balance. Use record matching to propose candidates, then validate names against Secretary of State records and addresses against dated business documents. A shared name alone never establishes ownership. For mergers, require a documented chain from the named owner to the current entity; for dissolved corporations, determine who can lawfully act before offering assistance. Keep issuer-held warrants in a separate queue with the issuer's replacement or reissuance procedure. Target sixty records with sufficient identity, authority, timing, and estimated fee evidence to support contact. That is a workload target, not a reason to relax eligibility. Independently sample twenty matches and require nineteen correct results before outreach. Also review every high-value or ambiguous match. The small audit supports a controlled pilot; it does not establish a precise population error rate or authorize unattended claims.

On Days 11–14, contact the first twenty eligible owners through individualized business letters or manually placed calls, then expand toward forty by Day 21. Each message identifies the recovery business, describes the property without exposing sensitive identifiers, states that the owner can claim directly through the treasury without hiring the service, and explains the proposed fee basis. Never imply government affiliation, exclusive access, or a deadline unsupported by the custodian. Give the owner the official treasury website and an independently verifiable callback route. For commercial email, apply 15 U.S.C. §7704 requirements where applicable, including accurate routing information, required identification, postal address, and effective opt-out handling. Do not introduce automated calls or texts without evaluating 47 CFR §64.1200 and applicable state requirements. Record delivered contacts, replies, two-way discussions, declines, and signed engagements separately. An unanswered message is not a conversation, and a returned envelope is not a delivered contact. Cap this pilot at two unanswered contact attempts per owner and suppress further outreach immediately after an objection. Customer distrust is measured through stated concerns, not dismissed as a sales objection.

Use the first ten two-way discussions to test whether the service solves a real administrative burden. Ask who controls historical records, whether the corporation has already filed, and which employee can authorize representation. Offer document assembly and status tracking rather than selling public search results as proprietary discoveries. A qualified mandate requires a valid agreement, a verified signer, lawful timing, a defensible ownership chain, and a fee estimate supported by available information. Exclude speculative amount bands from the mandate fee total until better evidence arrives. Model a $30,000 recovery at a lawful ten-percent fee as $3,000 of potential service revenue, not $30,000 of revenue. The illustration is usable only where that fee and agreement are permitted. Reserve $1,000 per eventual collected recovery for direct acquisition and handling, including allocated effort on unsuccessful files: $350 acquisition and $650 delivery. Those are underwriting assumptions to replace with cohort costs, not measured launch results. At a verified $10,000 recovery, the same fee produces only $1,000 and cannot carry that cost structure. Route such cases to direct claiming or redesign the workflow before accepting them. Do not hide weak unit economics behind a large aggregate property balance.

callout.title: Four Tactics That Reduce False Matches and Owner Distrust
callout.body: Experienced recovery operators sell documented execution, not secrecy around publicly accessible property searches.
items: Preserve historical holder and address details before refreshing a treasury search; current registry addresses alone often cannot explain an old corporate warrant.
Ask the corporate controller about existing claims before building a packet, preventing duplicate submissions and avoidable disputes over who performed the recovery work.
Send the official treasury claim route with the first substantive message; an owner who independently verifies the property becomes a better-qualified prospect.
Batch document requests by signer and entity, but retain separate property identifiers, fee calculations, and status histories for every claim.

sections.heading: 3. Days 15–21: Submit Evidence-Complete Claims and Reconcile the Fee Engine
paragraphs: Days 15–17 convert signed mandates into reviewable claim packets. The claims contractor checks the treasury's current instructions against the corporation's legal name, taxpayer identifier where required, historical address, signer authority, and property identifiers. Obtain sensitive documents through the restricted repository rather than ordinary email attachments. California Civil Code §1798.81.5 supplies a concrete reasonable-security requirement where applicable; apply access minimization across the entire workflow rather than treating security as a state-specific afterthought. E-signature software such as DocuSign can record execution evidence, but it does not make an ineligible agreement valid or replace a treasury's notarization requirement. The founder independently reviews identity and authority before submission. Track four distinct events: internal packet completion, submission receipt, custodian confirmation of intake, and claim determination. In this chapter, an accepted packet means the custodian has acknowledged intake without a currently identified missing item; it does not mean the claim is approved. If the agency offers only an automated receipt, retain that narrower status and do not inflate the accepted-packet count. A submission queue can be automated; authority to attest facts cannot be delegated to an unreviewed matching rule.

On Days 18–19, establish status tracking without overwhelming the treasury or the pod. Record the agency's published processing guidance and assign the next inquiry from that guidance, not an invented seven-day escalation cycle. Store each request for additional evidence with its exact wording, received date, owner, and response deadline. Separate owner delay, agency delay, and operator defect because each requires a different remedy. An incorrect identifier or missing required authority document is an operator defect; a queue awaiting agency review is not. Aim for at most one material operator defect among the first ten submitted packets, while reporting the actual count whenever fewer than ten exist. Freeze related submissions immediately after an identity or unauthorized-signature error, regardless of the aggregate rate. The founder reviews a daily exception queue capped at five active document-chasing cases. Contractors work from explicit tasks and time allowances, not open-ended instructions to investigate everything. By Day 21, target forty delivered contacts, ten substantive discussions, four qualified mandates, and two accepted packets. These are pilot thresholds rather than revenue predictions. If agency acknowledgments are unavailable, retain the evidence-complete submissions and classify that part of the expansion decision as pending.

Days 20–21 also reconcile the economic model to the canonical scorecard. At the illustrative $3,000 earned fee, twenty annual completed recoveries generate $60,000 Conservative revenue; eighty-five generate $255,000 Base revenue; and 150 generate $450,000 Scaled revenue. The associated client property totals would be $600,000, $2,550,000, and $4,500,000 at a uniform ten-percent fee, but none belongs in operator revenue. With $1,000 direct cost per collected recovery, direct costs are $20,000, $85,000, and $150,000. Other annual operating costs of $25,000, $74,375, and $75,000 produce total expenses of $45,000, $159,375, and $225,000. Subtracting those expenses yields exactly $15,000, $95,625, and $225,000 owner net profit, or 25%, 37.5%, and 50%. This allocation illustrates the supplied totals; it is not an independently established staffing-cost forecast. Conservative and Base retain one full-time operator plus two contractors; Scaled requires two full-time operators plus three contractors. Do not represent the five-person outcome as achievable by the launch pod automatically. Track earned fees, invoices, and cash receipts separately under the adopted accounting policy. A signed contingency agreement or treasury receipt does not itself establish earned revenue, and client principal must never subsidize the operator's runway.
