sections.heading: 4. Days 22–30 and Beyond: Apply Kill, Fix, or Scale Decisions to Mature Evidence
paragraphs: Days 22–30 close the pilot's evidence gaps instead of manufacturing a launch victory. Day 22 reconciles duplicates and contact delivery; Day 23 closes outstanding owner-document requests; Day 24 rechecks contracting restrictions; Day 25 audits packet defects; Day 26 updates the cash forecast; Day 27 evaluates fee sensitivity; Day 28 independently reviews the cohort; Day 29 drafts the decision memo; and Day 30 records Kill, Fix, or Scale by segment. Use cumulative delivered unique-owner contacts as the mandate conversion denominator: forty at Day 30, eighty at Day 60, and 120 at Day 90. Do not count repeated follow-ups as additional prospects. Target at least 10% qualified mandate conversion, producing four, eight, and twelve mandates respectively. Target two, four, and six accepted packets at those checkpoints. Underfilled samples default to Fix or continued observation, never a claimed statistical victory. Report matching precision on independent twenty-record audits separately from outreach conversion. Count all identity or authority incidents explicitly, even after correction. The decision memo must name the owner, evidence, spend authorization, and next review date for each continuing workstream so contractors do not interpret silence as permission to expand.

Kill means stop the defective segment or acquisition method, not abandon valid customer obligations. Any confirmed unauthorized filing, knowingly false ownership assertion, or prohibited fee arrangement stops affected activity immediately. Commercial Kill requires both adequate observation and persistently weak economics: below 5% qualified conversion at the checkpoint's contact denominator, plus projected fees below 1.5 times fully loaded direct cost. At Day 30 this is a provisional segment stop; retest only after a documented change. At Days 60 and 90, require a completed fourteen-day corrective experiment before treating the same commercial result as persistent. Fix covers conversion from 5% to below 10%, incomplete sample sizes, document bottlenecks, and unsettled agency acknowledgments. Change one variable per experiment, such as claimant type, evidence request sequence, or the explanation of paid assistance. Scale requires every listed quality, economics, runway, and capacity condition; good sales cannot offset bad identity controls. Increase new-contact volume by at most 25% after Day 30 and 50% after later checkpoints, subject to contractor hours. These increments authorize controlled prospecting only. They do not authorize hiring the five-person Scaled team or treating pending fees as spendable money.

Day 60 and Day 90 reviews must distinguish collection latency from business failure. With a canonical 3–12-month first-deal interval, zero receipts at ninety days alone does not justify Kill. Compare each pending claim with its custodian's published guidance, outstanding evidence, and documented queue position where available. For provisional expansion, require estimated lawful fees at least twice modeled fully loaded direct costs and at least 1.5 times those costs after a 25% fee reduction. The $3,000 fee and $1,000 cost illustration passes both tests, but observed failed-file effort can overturn it. Recalculate costs using actual hours and prospect acquisition spending, including work on unsuccessful cases. Retain six months of maintenance cash after every new commitment. Before permanent staffing expansion, require three collected recoveries, actual cohort contribution of at least 50% of earned fees after direct costs, and twelve weeks of measured capacity data. Three outcomes provide an initial calibration, not mature loss-rate evidence. If collections remain pending, continue the capped pilot only while runway and case evidence support it. Recognize revenue only when earned under the adopted policy; reconcile invoices and receipts separately. The correct Day 90 decision can be a disciplined Fix with viable claims, bounded spending, and no revenue yet.
